items.title: Aurelius Atlas
items.text:
Data governance made simple. Aurelius Atlas is an open-source data governance solution that enables business users to find, understand, and trust their data without waiting on IT: discover data assets and their context in seconds, see who is accountable for them and whether they are fit for purpose, follow the journey and transformations of data across systems, and keep sensitive information in line with regulations such as GDPR.

It is one all-in-one data catalogue, designed to be business-user-friendly, meeting the demands of modern distributed data environments.

This repository builds the new engine behind that product: a Python re-implementation of Apache Atlas that keeps the Atlas 2.4.0 REST API and the Atlas dashboard, with Elasticsearch 9 as the only backend instead of JanusGraph, HBase and Solr — so the catalogue is far easier to run and cheaper to operate. The original Java Atlas is converted in small, reviewed increments, each proven against the Atlas 2.4.0 source code, so the clients, integrations, and dashboards organisations rely on keep working exactly as they do today.

Start with the User Guide for what the catalogue does for your organisation, the Conversion roadmap for plan and status, the Architecture overview for the system as it will stand, and the Contributor Guide to set up your machine.

The User Guide is intentionally short: until the conversion is complete, the Apache Atlas documentation describes the behaviour this system reproduces, and every intended difference is listed in Deviations from Apache Atlas.

items.title: About the team
items.text: This project is maintained by the Aurelius Enterprise team. Please feel free to reach out if you have any questions, need assistance, or would like to contribute.

items.title: API Reference
items.text:
Generated API documentation for the Aurelius Atlas workspace, rendered from the docstrings in each project by mkdocstrings. The prose for what a project is lives in its README.md; the wiring for how it is built and run lives in its AGENTS.md (ADR 003). This tree is the reference for what it exposes: classes, functions, signatures, and examples.

Each page doubles as that component's design documentation: the technology-specific detail of how the component works — settings and knob names, storage layout, protocol mechanics, ports, commands. The architecture trees state the technology-neutral properties the component must keep. A page's Design section carries this detail, with the ADR that owns each rule linked.

  • Apps — the services: the Atlas server and the template examples
  • Libs — the Python, Angular, and style libraries the apps consume

items.title: Apps
items.text: API reference for the workspace applications. The Atlas product is aurelius-atlas-server; the FastAPI and Angular examples are the template's demonstrations, kept until the conversion plan is done (DD-019) and then removed (ADR 050).

items.title: aurelius-atlas-fastapi-example
items.text: This is an example FastAPI application.

items.title: Usage
items.text:
Run the following command to start the application locally:

python -m aurelius_atlas_fastapi_example

This launches a Uvicorn server at http://127.0.0.1:8000.

items.title: Deployment
items.text: Deploy using the provided Dockerfile. By default, the app listens on http://0.0.0.0:8000.

items.title: enforce_auth_security pydantic-validator
items.text:
enforce_auth_security() -> Settings

Fail fast when a non-development deployment misconfigures authentication or authorization.

Two silent-downgrade paths are closed here:

  • A plaintext auth_server_url lets a network-path attacker serve a forged OpenID configuration / JWKS, which mints tokens this API would accept — the whole bearer-token scheme collapses. OAuth token endpoints elsewhere in the workspace are https-only for the same reason.
  • An empty auth_audience (no AUTH_CLIENT_ID, no explicit audience) would accept any token from the issuer, and an empty auth_write_role would authenticate every caller for mutating operations. Both must be explicit.

items.title: enforce_transport_security pydantic-validator
items.text:
enforce_transport_security() -> Settings

Fail fast when a non-development deployment runs with unverified transport.

The defaults (database_sslmode="prefer", empty tls_cert_file) are convenient for local development, where the TLS material lives in the project .env. Outside development they must be set explicitly: otherwise a deployment that forgets the variables silently downgrades to opportunistic/unverified TLS — credentials and tokens over a channel a network-path attacker can read or impersonate.

items.title: aurelius-atlas-frontend-example
items.text: This is an example frontend application built with Angular.

items.title: Deployment
items.text: Deploy using the provided Dockerfile. By default, the app listens on http://localhost:8080.

items.title: Configuration
items.text: The following configuration is required to run the application:

items.title: Client-Facing Configuration
items.text:
The application is configured at runtime via an externally mounted config.json file. This client-facing configuration file contains the necessary settings for the frontend to communicate with the backend and authentication services. Below is an example config.json file:

{
    "keycloak": {
        "clientId": "aurelius",
        "realm": "master",
        "url": "http://keycloak.localhost:8181"
    }
}

Mount the config.json file into the container at /usr/share/nginx/html/config.json via a Docker volume or Docker configs mechanism.

items.title: Nginx Configuration
items.text:
The production image already bundles the locale-aware Nginx configuration for the Angular app. The bundled file is served at /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf, and optional fragments may be added under /etc/nginx/app.d/*.conf inside the existing server block.

The image serves locale-prefixed routes (/en-US/, /nl-NL/), redirects / to the preferred language, and falls back to the matching locale's index.html for client-side routing. Keep the app-serving rules in the image and add only server-scoped proxy or TLS fragments via /etc/nginx/app.d/*.conf.

server {
    listen 8080;
    root /usr/share/nginx/html;

    include /etc/nginx/app.d/*.conf;

    set $accept_language en-US;
    location = / {
        if ($http_accept_language ~* "^nl") {
            set $accept_language nl-NL;
        }
        return 302 /$accept_language/$is_args$args;
    }

    location /en-US/ {
        try_files $uri $uri/ /en-US/index.html;
    }

    location /nl-NL/ {
        try_files $uri $uri/ /nl-NL/index.html;
    }

    location / {
        try_files $uri /en-US/index.html;
    }
}

Do not define another server block or an HTTP-level map in a fragment; the hardened image includes fragments at server scope only.

items.title: aurelius-atlas-server
items.text: The Aurelius Atlas server: the Apache Atlas 2.4.0 REST API on Elasticsearch.

items.title: Usage
items.text:
npx nx serve aurelius-atlas-server

This starts the dev Elasticsearch store and the observability stack, then the server at https://localhost:21000, the port Apache Atlas uses.

items.title: Deployment
items.text: Deploy the image built from the provided Dockerfile. It listens on port 21000 and needs the Elasticsearch settings; it does not start without its store.

items.title: Design
items.text:
The technology-specific detail of how the server runs. The properties it must keep are in the architecture: Configuration Management (ADR 018), Components & Interfaces.

Settings. Read once at start-up into a frozen ServerSettings; a validation failure (missing key, bad scheme, half a TLS pair) stops start-up with a message naming the variable (SRV-01, SRV-02). All names carry the AURELIUS_ATLAS_SERVER_ prefix. What a deployment must supply, with no defaults:

Variable Purpose ..._ELASTICSEARCH_HOSTS JSON list of store node URLs, e.g. ["https://es-0:9200"] — https only ..._ELASTICSEARCH_PASSWORD Store password — a SecretStr, never shown in logs ..._ELASTICSEARCH_CA_CERTS PEM CA of the store certificate; the store link is https-only (ADR 039) ..._TLS_CERT_FILE + ..._TLS_KEY_FILE PEM pair for serving HTTPS: both set, or both unset — enforced at start-up

With defaults: HOST (0.0.0.0 in the image), PORT (21000, Atlas's port — kept so existing clients find the catalogue where Atlas was, ADR 046), LOG_LEVEL, REVISION (reported by admin/version, ADM-01), DASHBOARD_DIR (None serves the API only, DSH-04), MODELS_DIR (default: the vendored Atlas 2.4.0 addons/models, MDL-16/DD-032), TYPEDEF_REFRESH_SECONDS (5.0 — how long the server answers from its type registry before checking for another process's type change, TDS-13/DD-029).

A half TLS pair stops the server from starting

TLS_CERT_FILE and TLS_KEY_FILE are both set, or both unset — the pairing is enforced at start-up. A container that mounts only the certificate exits with a message naming the missing variable; this is the design working, not a broken image.

The image (apps/aurelius-atlas-server/Dockerfile: hardened base, runs as nonroot) bakes in the production defaults — listen on 0.0.0.0:21000, dashboards served from /application/dashboard — and a liveness healthcheck against /api/atlas/admin/liveness that verifies the server's own certificate when TLS is on. Liveness is the probe a restart decision uses; readiness also fails while the store is away (DD-016).

Parity scenarios. scenarios/<resource>/*.scenario.yaml state each expectation as Atlas's own answer — e.g. scenarios/admin/version.scenario.yaml expects Version: "2.4.0", Name: apache-atlas, the exact content type — each cited to the Java source that produces it. Build-varying fields are marked volatile; the two places Aurelius Atlas must answer differently (name, description) carry a deviations: DV-03 entry. Anything else that differs fails the scenario (ADR 052).

items.title: Libs
items.text:
API reference for the workspace libraries, grouped by stack. Each library documents itself in its README.md; this tree lists what it exposes.

  • Python — the Atlas code: model, typesystem, core, store, tooling
  • Angular — the template frontend's data, UI, and observability libraries
  • Styles — design tokens shared by the Angular apps

items.title: Angular
items.text: The Angular libraries of the template frontend example: typed data access, shared UI components, and browser OpenTelemetry. They serve the example app and leave with it (DD-019); the Atlas dashboard itself is the vendored Apache Atlas dashboard, not Angular code from this workspace.

items.title: aurelius-atlas-data-access
items.text: This library provides common utilities for API data access in Angular projects.

items.title: API Documentation
items.text: This library is written in TypeScript, which is not covered by the generated API reference (mkdocstrings covers Python only here). The source code with its TSDoc comments is the API reference: source.

items.title: Installation
items.text: You can import aurelius-atlas-data-access in your Angular project directly from the monorepo. It will be bundled with your application code and tree-shaken to include only the parts you use.

items.title: aurelius-atlas-ui
items.text: This library provides common UI components for Angular projects.

items.title: API Documentation
items.text: This library is written in TypeScript, which is not covered by the generated API reference (mkdocstrings covers Python only here). Storybook, described below, is the component API reference; for the raw signatures, see the source.

items.title: Installation
items.text: You can import aurelius-atlas-ui in your Angular project directly from the monorepo. It will be bundled with your application code and tree-shaken to include only the parts you use.

items.title: Storybook
items.text:
The aurelius-atlas-ui library includes a Storybook instance for interactive documentation and testing of the UI components. To run Storybook, execute the following command in the root of the monorepo:

nx run aurelius-atlas-ui:storybook

This will start the Storybook server and open the Storybook interface in your default web browser, where you can explore and interact with the UI components provided by the aurelius-atlas-ui library.

items.title: Python
items.text: The Python workspace libraries. The Atlas spine — aurelius-atlas-model, aurelius-atlas-typesystem, aurelius-atlas-core, aurelius-atlas-store-es — plus the conversion tooling (parity, trace) and the template's example library and SDK (DD-019).

items.title: aurelius-atlas-core
items.text:
Atlas stores and services for Aurelius Atlas (DD-002). Since increment 1.4: the typedef store, which keeps type definitions in one Elasticsearch document and serves them from the type registry. Since 1.5: Apache Atlas's built-in models and their typedef patches, loaded at start-up. Since 1.6: the store's reads and the search of /v2/types/typedefs. Since 2.2: the entity store, which keeps each entity as one Elasticsearch document, reserves unique attribute values and writes several entities all or nothing through a journal (DD-043 to DD-048).

store = TypedefStore(TypeRegistry(), ElasticsearchTypedefDocument(elasticsearch_store.client))
await store.load()  # every stored definition into the registry
created = await store.create_types_def(types_def)
await store.refresh()  # pick up another process's change (at most every 5 s)
await ModelLoader(store).load(BUILTIN_MODELS_DIR)  # addons/models of Atlas 2.4.0, and their patches
store.get_by_name("hive_table")  # the registered definition, as resolution completed it
search_types_def(store.registry, TypeSearchFilter.from_query([("type", "ENTITY")]))  # each kind sorted by name

items.title: Installation
items.text:
dependencies = ["aurelius-atlas-core"]

[tool.uv.sources.aurelius-atlas-core]
workspace = true

items.title: Vendored models
items.text:
aurelius_atlas_core/models/ is addons/models of Apache Atlas release-2.4.0, byte for byte (DD-032). To prove it, compare it with the tag:

diff -r <apache-atlas checkout at release-2.4.0>/addons/models libs/python/aurelius-atlas-core/aurelius_atlas_core/models

items.title: aurelius_atlas_core.typedef_store
items.text:
The typedef store: type definitions kept in Elasticsearch and served from the registry (TDS-01 to TDS-13).

Ported from AtlasTypeDefGraphStore and its def stores (Atlas*DefStoreV2) of Apache Atlas 2.4.0. A change is tried on the registry's transient copy, checked as Atlas's def stores check it, written as one document (DD-028) and only then committed to the registry (TDS-10). The document also holds the record of each typedef patch, written with the patch's change (DD-031).

Type Aliases:

  • TypeUsage –

    Whether entities, classifications or relationships of a type exist (DD-030).

Classes:

  • PatchChange –

    What a typedef patch decided (MDL-07): its status, and the definitions it updates, if any.

  • TypedefStore –

    Type definitions kept in a TypedefDocument, served from a TypeRegistry (AtlasTypeDefGraphStore).

Functions:

  • is_newer_version –

    ObjectUtils.compare(new, old) > 0: compared as strings, an absent version less than any (MDL-02).

  • is_valid_name –

    A letter, then letters, digits, spaces or _; optionally after __ (isValidName, TDS-02).

  • java_compare –

    Compare as Java's String.compareTo does: by UTF-16 code unit (MDL-01, MDL-02).

  • never_in_use –

    The type usage until the entity store exists (2.2): no type is in use (DD-030).

  • rectify –

    Repair what older stores allowed, as rectifyTypeErrorsIfAny does on load (TDS-12).

  • referenced_type_names –

    The type names inside array<…> and map<…,…> (AtlasTypeUtil.getReferencedTypeNames, TDS-04).

  • types_def_of –

    An AtlasTypesDef holding typedefs, each in the list of its kind.

  • types_to_create –

    The definitions whose name is not registered, as any kind or built-in (getTypesToCreate, MDL-02).

  • types_to_update –

    The definitions registered as the same kind, when newer (getTypesToUpdate, MDL-02).

Attributes:

    The patch action under which an update may add mandatory attributes (TYPEDEF_PATCH_ADD_MANDATORY_ATTRIBUTE).

items.title: apply_patch async
items.text:
apply_patch(patch: AtlasPatch, decide: Callable[[TypeRegistry], PatchChange]) -> PatchStatus | None

Apply a typedef patch unless its record says it is done, and record how it ended (MDL-05, MDL-06).

decide looks at the registry and says what the patch does; an AtlasError from it, or from the update it asks for, makes the patch FAILED, and leaves the definitions as they were. Any other error is raised. The patch's record is written with its change (DD-031); a patch without an id is not recorded.

items.title: aurelius_atlas_core.entity_store
items.text:
EntityStore: entities by GUID and unique attributes, written all or nothing (ENS-02 to ENS-09).

The storage side of AtlasEntityStoreV2 and EntityGraphMapper: what a graph transaction gave Atlas, rebuilt on Elasticsearch with reserved unique values, conditional writes and a journal (DD-044 to DD-048).

  • EntityWriteError –

items.title: aurelius_atlas_core.entity_documents
items.text:
The entities' documents in Elasticsearch: entities, unique value reservations and the write journal (ENS-01).

The I/O behind EntityStore: reads in real time, conditional writes, create-only reservations (DD-043 to DD-047). Documents go to Elasticsearch as the bytes of Atlas's JSON codec, so values keep their digits (DD-039).

Classes:

  • ElasticsearchEntityDocuments –

    EntityDocuments in three Elasticsearch indices behind aliases (DD-043, DD-045, DD-046).

  • EntityDocuments –

    Where EntityStore keeps entities, reservations and its journal.

  • JournalEntry –

    A write in flight: its id, lease, the entities' states before it, its reservations, releases and removals.

  • Reservation –

    A unique value held by an entity: the key's id, the holder's GUID and the write that reserved it (DD-045).

  • VersionedEntity –

    A stored entity and the version it was read in (DD-047).

  • WriteResult –

    How one entity of a bulk write ended: written, or failed by a version conflict or another error.

Attributes:

  • ENTITY_INDEX –

    The alias of the entity index (DD-043).

  • ENTITY_MAPPING (dict[str, Any]) –

    System properties and referenced GUIDs mapped for exact lookup; attribute values stored, not indexed, until 4.1.

  • INDEX_PREFIX –

    The prefix of the three aliases; tests give their own.

  • JOURNAL_INDEX –

    The alias of the write journal (DD-046).

  • JOURNAL_PAGE –

    How many journal entries recovery reads at once; a live journal holds one entry per write in flight.

  • REFERRING_PAGE –

    How many referring entities one search page holds (DD-057).

  • UNIQUE_VALUE_INDEX –

    The alias of the unique value reservations (DD-045).

Atlas's built-in models and their typedef patches, loaded at start-up (MDL-01 to MDL-15).

Ported from AtlasTypeDefStoreInitializer of Apache Atlas 2.4.0. Each model file and each patch is one change of the typedef store, decided on the newest stored definitions (DD-033); a patch's record is written with its change (DD-031).

items.title: aurelius_atlas_core.stored_form
items.text:
What Atlas keeps of a type definition, and so answers with afterwards (TDS-03, TDS-05 to TDS-07).

Atlas's def stores write a definition to a graph vertex and build every response from the vertex again (toEntityDef(vertex), …). Attributes go through the legacy form of toJsonFromAttribute and toAttributeDefFromJson; these functions apply the same round trip without the graph (DD-028).

Functions:

  • java_end_string –

    AtlasRelationshipEndDef.toString, as RELATIONSHIPDEF_INVALID_END*_UPDATE messages show it (TDS-08).

  • stamp_created –

    createTypeVertex: fill in what a new definition lacks (TDS-03); changes typedef, as Java does.

  • stamp_updated –

    updateTypeVertex and markVertexUpdated: keep what may not change, bump the version (TDS-07).

  • stored_attribute –

    An attribute after toJsonFromAttribute and toAttributeDefFromJson (TDS-05).

  • stored_typedef –

    The definition as Atlas reads it back from its vertex (to*Def(vertex), TDS-05, TDS-06).

Attributes:

    Integer.MAX_VALUE: the upper bound Atlas stores for an unbounded list or set.

  • LEGACY_KIND –

    The legacy DataTypes.TypeCategory names Atlas's TYPE_MATCH_FAILED messages use (TDS-02).

type_ is the definition's resolved type, whose attributes are stored; None for an enum.

items.title: avro_schema classmethod
items.text:
avro_schema(*args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> dict[str, Any]

Return the Avro schema with datetime fields encoded as timestamp-millis.

pydantic-avro defaults date-time fields to timestamp-micros, but the Confluent Avro converter maps only timestamp-millis to the Connect Timestamp logical type. Without it, consumers that read through that converter (e.g. the Debezium JDBC sink) see a nameless raw INT64 and try to bind it to a timestamptz column as a bigint, which fails.

items.title: aurelius-atlas-model
items.text:
Atlas data shapes for Aurelius Atlas, without I/O (DD-002). Since increment 1.1: the Apache Atlas 2.4.0 type definitions (enum, struct, classification, entity, relationship and business metadata), their header and AtlasTypesDef, as Pydantic models that read and write Atlas's REST JSON. Since 1.5: the patch record AtlasPatch. Since 2.1a: the entity models of aurelius_atlas_model.instance, one module per Atlas class (AtlasEntity, AtlasEntityWithExtInfo, AtlasEntityHeader, AtlasClassification, AtlasObjectId, EntityMutationResponse, …), and the JSON conventions all models share in aurelius_atlas_model.base. Since 2.1b: Atlas's JSON codec, aurelius_atlas_model.codec, which keeps the digits of decimals.

from aurelius_atlas_model.typedef import AtlasTypesDef

types = AtlasTypesDef.model_validate(request_body)  # Atlas's normalisations apply
response_body = types.to_json()  # Java names, nulls left out, epoch-millisecond dates

from aurelius_atlas_model.instance import AtlasEntitiesWithExtInfo

entities = AtlasEntitiesWithExtInfo.model_validate(request_body)  # entities without a GUID get "-<n>"

items.title: aurelius_atlas_model.typedef
items.text:
Atlas type definitions as Pydantic models that read and write Atlas's REST JSON (DD-020).

Ported from org.apache.atlas.model.typedef of Apache Atlas 2.4.0. Field names are snake_case in Python and the Java getter names in JSON (TDM-01). The normalisations the Java setters and constructors apply run as validators, so they hold for request bodies and for models built in code alike.

Type Aliases:

  • AttributeDefs –

    attributeDefs: never null, one definition per name (TDM-06, TDM-07).

Classes:

  • AtlasAttributeDef –

    An attribute of a struct, classification, entity, relationship or business metadata type (TDM-10).

  • AtlasBaseTypeDef –

    What every type definition has: identity, audit fields, name and options.

  • AtlasBusinessMetadataDef –

    A business metadata type: attributes that apply to the entity types its options name.

  • AtlasClassificationDef –

    A classification type: attributes, super types and the entity types it may be applied to.

  • AtlasConstraintDef –

    A constraint on an attribute, such as ownedRef or inverseRef.

  • AtlasEntityDef –

    An entity type.

  • AtlasEnumDef –

    An enum type.

  • AtlasEnumElementDef –

    One value of an enum type.

  • AtlasRelationshipAttributeDef –

    An entity attribute that a relationship type adds; read-only, derived from the relationship types.

  • AtlasRelationshipDef –

    A relationship type between two entity types (TDM-12).

  • AtlasRelationshipEndDef –

    One end of a relationship type: the entity type there and the attribute it gets (TDM-12).

  • AtlasStructDef –

    A struct type, and the base of the types that have attributes.

  • AtlasTypeDefHeader –

    The identity of a type definition, as /v2/types/typedefs/headers lists it.

  • AtlasTypesDef –

    Type definitions of every kind: the body of /v2/types/typedefs (TDM-13).

    How many values an attribute or relationship end holds.

  • IndexType –

    How an attribute is indexed.

  • PropagateTags –

    The direction in which classifications propagate over a relationship.

    How the two ends of a relationship depend on each other.

items.title: aurelius_atlas_model.codec
items.text:
Atlas's JSON: numbers with a fraction read as decimals, decimals and dates written as Jackson writes them.

Atlas's REST mapper reads floats as BigDecimal (USE_BIG_DECIMAL_FOR_FLOATS) and writes a BigDecimal with its digits and a Date as epoch milliseconds (VAL-01, DD-039).

Functions:

  • dumps –

    Write value as Atlas's REST mapper does, compactly, in UTF-8 (VAL-01).

  • loads –

    Read JSON as Jackson does with USE_BIG_DECIMAL_FOR_FLOATS: every float is a Decimal with its digits.

Attributes:

  • NOT_JSON_ERROR –

items.title: dumps
items.text:
dumps(value: Any) -> bytes

Write value as Atlas's REST mapper does, compactly, in UTF-8 (VAL-01).

A Decimal keeps its digits, a datetime is epoch milliseconds, NaN and infinities are strings, a model is its to_json, and map keys are Java's text of the key.

items.text:
to_json() -> dict[str, Any]

The JSON Atlas writes for this model: Java names, null fields left out, empty ones kept (TDM-02).

Untyped values keep their Python types (Decimal, datetime) for codec.dumps (VAL-01, DD-039).

items.title: aurelius-atlas-parity
items.text: Parity scenarios for Aurelius Atlas: the scenario format, the runner and the comparison.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
Part of the workspace dev group, which loads the pytest plugin into every test run.

[dependency-groups]
dev = ["aurelius-atlas-parity"]

[tool.uv.sources.aurelius-atlas-parity]
workspace = true

items.title: aurelius_atlas_parity
items.text:
Parity scenarios: requests with the responses Apache Atlas 2.4.0 gives, run against Aurelius Atlas (ADR 052).

Modules:

  • compare –

    The exact comparison of a response body with its expectation (SCN-09, SCN-10, SCN-12; DD-013).

  • path –

    Paths into a JSON document: the JSONPath subset $, .name, ['name'], [n] and [*] (SCN-07).

  • plugin –

    The pytest plugin: gives each scenario test its endpoints and deviations as test properties (SCN-14; DD-014).

  • run –

    Running a scenario: send each stage's request, compare its response, save values (SCN-05 to SCN-12).

  • scenario –

    The scenario format: *.scenario.yaml files, read and validated (SCN-01 to SCN-03; DD-012).

  • testing –

    A sample ASGI application for this library's own tests.

Classes:

  • Scenario –

    One scenario file (SCN-01).

  • ScenarioError –

    A scenario file does not parse or does not match the format (SCN-03).

  • ScenarioFailedError –

    A stage's response differs from its expectation; the message lists every difference (SCN-11).

Functions:

  • load_scenarios –

    Read every *.scenario.yaml below a directory as pytest parameters, one test per scenario (SCN-04).

  • run_scenario –

    Run a scenario's stages in order through the client (SCN-05); {run} is unique to the run (SCN-16).

  • run_scenario –

    Run a scenario's stages in order through the client (SCN-05); {run} is unique to the run (SCN-16).

items.title: substitute
items.text:
substitute(value: Any, saved: Mapping[str, Any]) -> Any

Replace {name} by saved values in every string of a JSON value (SCN-06).

A string that is exactly {name} becomes the saved value with its JSON type; elsewhere the value is written into the string. Object keys are strings, so a value written into one is its text. {{ and }} stand for literal braces.

    A name was not saved by an earlier stage.

items.title: setup_logger
items.text:
setup_logger(level: int | str = INFO) -> None

Set up logging for the application with a standardized log output format.

This function configures the logging system to use the specified logging level, with a custom log format that includes the timestamp, log level, logger name, and log message. Log levels can be provided as either an integer or a string corresponding to standard logging levels.

  • CRITICAL
  • ERROR
  • WARNING
  • INFO
  • DEBUG

Parameters:

Examples:

Set up logging with the default level. This will log messages with a level of INFO and above.

>>> setup_logging()

Set up logging to show DEBUG-level messages (and above) by providing the logging level's integer value.

>>> setup_logging(logging.DEBUG)

Set up logging by specifying the logging level as a string. This is equivalent to the previous example.

>>> setup_logging("DEBUG")

TLS_POSTGRES_HOST = 'localhost'

Host test clients connect to.

The ephemeral certificates cover only loopback names and libpq verifies the host parameter against them, so clients connect to localhost through the published port rather than to get_container_host_ip() (a bridge/gateway address in some Docker setups). items.title: configure_tls_postgres
items.text:
configure_tls_postgres(container: PostgresContainer, certs: TlsCertificates) -> None

Configure a PostgreSQL test container to enforce TLS, mirroring dev/postgres.

Call before the container starts. The server comes up with ssl=on and a hostssl-only pg_hba.conf, so plaintext TCP connections are rejected server-side; clients connect with sslmode=verify-full against certs.ca_bundle_path (host: :data:TLS_POSTGRES_HOST).

The hardened image runs as a fixed non-root user that cannot read host-owned key material it does not own, so — like dev/postgres — the certificates are copied into the container filesystem with strict permissions before startup (Postgres also refuses world-readable keys).

items.title: tls_certificates
items.text:
tls_certificates(*, prefix: str = 'aurelius-tls', sans: Sequence[str] = DEFAULT_TLS_SANS) -> Generator[TlsCertificates]

Generate ephemeral TLS material, removing the directory again on exit.

A throwaway CA and server certificate (SANs: sans) live in a temporary directory - named with prefix - for the duration of the block, keeping the fixture as hermetic as the random credentials next to it; no certgen/decrypt is needed to run tests.

Parameters:

Usage in a fixture::

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def db_tls_material() -> Generator[TlsCertificates]:
    with tls_certificates() as certs:
        yield certs

items.title: aurelius-atlas-typesystem
items.text:
The Atlas type system for Aurelius Atlas, without I/O (DD-002): the type registry and the types that type definitions resolve to. Since increment 1.2: the built-in, array, map, enum and struct types, attribute types and constraints. Since 1.3: entity and classification hierarchies, relationship and business metadata types. Since 2.1b: the value side of the built-in, enum, array and map types, as Atlas checks, normalises and compares attribute values. Since 2.1c: the same for structs, classifications (with their validity periods) and entities (with their relationship attributes).

from aurelius_atlas_typesystem.registry import TypeRegistry

registry = TypeRegistry()
with registry.update() as transient:  # committed when the block ends, discarded when it raises
    transient.add_types(types_def)  # resolves every type; raises AtlasError on a bad reference
registry.entity_type("hive_table")

int_type = registry.get_type("int")
int_type.get_normalized_value("42")  # 42; Java's Integer.valueOf rules, None when invalid
registry.get_type("array<int>").validate_value(["x"], "a", messages := [])  # messages: a[0]=x: invalid value…
registry.entity_type("hive_table").validate_value(entity, "entity", messages)  # e.g. mandatory attribute missing

This module re-exports them and makes the unresolved type of a definition (type_of).

    boolean: a boolean, or true or false in any case.

  • BuiltInType –

    A primitive type such as string or int, of the atlas_core service type (TRG-01).

  • ByteType –

    byte: a 8-bit Java integer.

  • DateType –

    date: a number of milliseconds since the epoch, or a date in Atlas's serialized format, in UTC.

  • DoubleType –

    double: a number within ±Double.MAX_VALUE, held as a Python float.

  • FloatType –

    float: a number within ±Float.MAX_VALUE, held as the shortest decimal of its 32-bit value.

  • IntType –

    int: a 32-bit Java integer.

  • LongType –

    long: a 64-bit Java integer.

  • ObjectIdType –

    objectid: a reference to an entity of object_type, by GUID or by unique attributes.

  • ShortType –

    short: a 16-bit Java integer.

  • StringType –

    string: every value, as Java's text of it.

items.title: aurelius_atlas_typesystem.java
items.text:
Java's number conversions, on Java values held as Python values (DD-040).

A Java Integer, Long or BigInteger is an int, a BigDecimal a Decimal, a Double a float and a Float a float holding the shortest decimal of its 32-bit value. A bool is a Java Boolean, never a number. Each function is named after the Java method it ports.

Type Aliases:

  • JavaNumber –

Functions:

  • big_decimal_value_of –

    BigDecimal.valueOf(double): the decimal of Double.toString (5 becomes 5.0).

  • double_value –

    Number.doubleValue: the number as Java's double (an infinity beyond its range).

  • float_value –

    Number.floatValue: the number as Java's float (an infinity beyond its range).

  • is_long –

    Whether value is an integer Jackson reads as an Integer or a Long, not a BigInteger.

  • is_number –

    value instanceof Number: an int, float or Decimal, but not a bool.

  • is_valid_time_zone –

    AtlasClassificationType.isValidTimeZone: GMT, or an id TimeZone resolves to another zone.

  • long_value –

    Number.longValue: a BigInteger or BigDecimal wraps to 64 bits; a double saturates, NaN is 0.

  • parse_big_decimal –

    new BigDecimal(String): sign, digits with an optional point, an optional exponent; else None.

  • parse_double –

    Double.valueOf(String): trimmed; sign; decimal or hexadecimal; NaN; Infinity; a type suffix.

  • parse_float –

    Float.valueOf(String): as parse_double, rounded to Java's float.

  • parse_long –

    Long.valueOf(String) and its kin: an optional sign and ASCII digits, or None.

  • time_zone –

    TimeZone.getTimeZone(id), or None for an id Java does not know (EVL-07, DD-042).

  • to_big_integer –

    AtlasBuiltInTypes.toBigInteger: an integer as it is, a decimal or a double truncated toward zero.

  • to_float32 –

    Round a double to Java's float and hold it as the shortest decimal of the 32-bit value (DD-040).

Attributes:

  • DOUBLE_MAX –

    Double.MAX_VALUE.

  • DOUBLE_MIN –

    Double.MIN_VALUE, the smallest positive double.

  • FLOAT_MAX –

    Float.MAX_VALUE, exactly, as a double.

  • FLOAT_MIN –

    Float.MIN_VALUE, the smallest positive float, as a double.

  • SHORT_ZONE_IDS –

    Java's legacy three-letter time zone ids that the tz database lacks, and the zones Java maps them to

items.title: to_float32

to_float32(value: float) -> float

Round a double to Java's float and hold it as the shortest decimal of the 32-bit value (DD-040).

A value beyond Float.MAX_VALUE becomes an infinity, as Java's narrowing conversion does.

items.title: Styles
items.text: Design tokens shared by the Angular apps: aurelius-atlas-brand provides the Bulma-based theme the template's example frontend and aurelius-atlas-ui components are styled with.

items.title: aurelius-atlas-brand
items.text: This library provides the Aurelius brand styles and assets for use in Aurelius projects.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
You can include aurelius-atlas-brand styles in your project by adding them to your root styles.scss file:

@use "@aurelius/atlas-brand/src/main";

Then, you can include the aurelius-atlas-brand assets in your project by adding the following to your angular.json:

{
    "assets": [
        {
            "source": "libs/styles/aurelius-atlas-brand/assets",
            "target": "assets/aurelius-atlas-brand"
        }
    ]
}

Ensure the path points to the correct location of the aurelius-atlas-brand library.

items.title: Architecture
items.text:
Aurelius Atlas helps an organisation discover, understand, and trust its data — and stays easy to run, because a catalogue that is expensive to operate governs nothing. The engine behind that is a Python re-implementation of Apache Atlas 2.4.0 with Elasticsearch 9 as its only store. The two working records of the system are the conversion roadmap — the increments, their status and their semantics specs — and the architecture decisions, the ADRs that constrain every change. Both are kept current by every pull request.

What is a 'working record'?

A page that states the system's current truth and is updated by the pull requests that change it — unlike a reference page, which describes a planned state and is written once, by the increment that builds it. If a working record and the code disagree, the record is wrong.

The remaining trees are the reference architecture: they describe the system as it will stand when the plan is done. They are written increment by increment — each page names the increment that writes it, so a page is written in the pull request of that increment, while its facts are fresh (ADR 051). Pages not yet written carry a Planned marker naming their increment; the convention is in Documentation.

Why two kinds of pages

A mid-conversion system has no single accurate description: the code is the plan partly built. Splitting the records (what is true now, maintained by every PR) from the reference (what will be true, written as each increment lands) keeps both statements honest — each page names the increment, spec, or code that owns its facts.

items.title: The trees
items.text:
Tree Subject Written by Vision & Strategy Why the system exists, for whom, and where it is going written (ADRs 046–052, the roadmap) Data Lifecycle Management How catalogue data enters, lives, is shared, and is retired 0.2 → 6.3, per page Data Governance Types, lineage, quality, ownership, auditability 1.6 → 6.2, per page Platform Connectivity, delivery, observability, resilience, security 0.2 → 6.4, per page

Each tree index page carries its own per-page filling map.

These pages state the system's properties by role — the search store, the identity provider, the collector — so the description survives a change of product. The knobs, ports, and commands of each part live in its own documentation: the API Reference pages (design documentation per component), the Contributor Guide (cross-cutting how-tos), and each dev/ slice's README (development topology).

items.title: Architecture Decisions
items.text: This section records architecture decisions as Architecture Decision Records (ADRs): short documents that capture a decision, the business situation that forced it, and the consequences it has. Code tells you what was built; an ADR tells you why — and the why is the part code cannot hand over.

items.title: The decision log
items.text:
New here? This is the whole set in one table. Read the records that govern the area you are about to work in; the rest can wait.

# Decision Status 001 Keep one monorepo for every stack — one repository, one entry point, atomic cross-stack change. Accepted 002 Modules are removable as whole slices — spine or optional capability, deleted in one pass. Accepted 003 Every project documents itself — knowledge beside what it describes, no central catalogue. Accepted 004 One shared domain model — one canonical definition per concept, generated or checked everywhere. Accepted 005 Development infrastructure starts with the app — one command to a running system. Accepted 006 The whole system runs on one machine — defects reproducible locally, validation without operated infrastructure. Accepted 007 One shared identity provider — one place people exist; surfaces only verify what it issues. Accepted 008 Real secrets encrypted, dev defaults committed — ciphertext travels with the code. Accepted 009 Every example runs and is tested — a broken example is removed, not annotated. Accepted 010 The unit validated is the unit that ships — one build per change, environments differ by settings only. Accepted 011 The development environment is a versioned artifact — one base for people and pipelines. Accepted 012 Validation runs against real services — a passing test is evidence about the shipped path. Accepted 013 Services prove who they are at every boundary — machine identity, separate from human identity. Accepted 014 The gate is defined once — the same rule set runs at commit time and in the pipeline. Accepted 015 A change answers for what it caused — change-caused findings block; world-state findings are reviewed on a cadence. Accepted 016 The system observes itself — traces, metrics, and logs never leave the boundary. Accepted 017 Shared concepts change only compatibly — additive by default, a breaking change becomes a new version. Accepted 018 Settings arrive at startup through one channel — read once, validated, failing loudly. Accepted 019 The system releases as one versioned whole — one number, one changelog, one release event. Accepted 020 Dependencies stay current by default — routine updates automatic, framework majors planned. Accepted 021 A new technology joins by recipe — discovered, gated, releasable, removable in one pass. Accepted 022 The codebase explains itself to its agents — nearest-first instructions for machine readers. Accepted 023 A storage schema changes only by recorded migration — one ordered path, data moved rather than replaced. Proposed 024 A validated release is promoted by a declared path — dev and test are the system's; beyond that, the deployment's. Accepted 025 Data has a stated lifetime — every kind expires on a named schedule the system enforces. Proposed 026 The system can be brought back from a named snapshot — backups stated, recovery rehearsed, loss bounded. Proposed 027 Every stream carries a stated delivery guarantee — duplication and loss decided per stream, not defaulted. Proposed 028 Operational secret handling has a named owner — rotation, loss, and break-glass rehearsed, not invented. Accepted 029 What ships is signed and its origin provable — verification is part of delivery, not a later hope. Accepted 030 Interfaces between parts are verified, not assumed — the agreement is stated once and drift fails the change. Accepted 031 Runtime versions have a declared support window — one answer per runtime, bumps planned, nothing floating. Accepted 032 Shared streams are named by a declared convention — the name says what flows and which version, never where. Accepted 033 Shipped artifacts carry a contents inventory — what is in what we ran is a lookup, not a reconstruction. Accepted 034 Signals meet at one replaceable collection point — parts export to a seam, never to a backend directly. Accepted 035 Parts hand work through a durable event log — the log is the default integration; joining is a subscription. Accepted 036 The delivery plane is a named exception to the data boundary — the pipeline crosses at recorded points; the running system never does. Accepted 037 The system itself promises nothing about staying up — availability is what the deployment builds around it. Accepted 038 What a person may do is decided in one place — permission apart from identity; one answer, one act to revoke. Proposed 039 Data is protected where it travels and rests — declared arrangements, not assumed properties. Accepted 040 The system raises its hand when it is broken — named triggers, named destinations; silence is a condition. Proposed 041 A failure of the running system has an owner and a rehearsed path — response owned, written, practised. Accepted 042 Every dataset has an owner who answers for it — sharing is a stated answer, never an absence. Proposed 043 AI-assisted review informs the two signatures — it does not replace them, and its findings follow the blocking rule. Accepted 044 Every change carries two human signatures — the task owner who answers for it and a reviewer who confirms understanding. Accepted 045 Conventions are borrowed before they are invented — framework, then community, then invention; the preference outlives the brands. Accepted 046 The catalogue keeps its public contract while its implementation is replaced; every visible difference is a recorded deviation. Accepted 047 One search store is the only system of record for metadata — no separate graph, relational store or index. Accepted 048 Behaviour is proven against recorded responses of the reference implementation before it is accepted. Superseded by 052 049 Every function and every specified rule is traceable to a test, and the trace is published per change. Accepted 050 The system carries only the capabilities the catalogue needs — a named deviation from the template spine. Accepted 051 The conversion proceeds in increments, each defined by a written specification before it is built. Accepted 052 Behaviour is specified by scenarios read from the reference source and its tests, each citing where; the reference is never run. Proposed

items.title: Why record decisions
items.text:
• Decisions are inherited. Every codebase is read first by people who were not in the room — onboarding, handover, a fork. Without the reasoning, they cannot tell a deliberate constraint from an accident, and "fix" decisions that were the whole point.
  • Decisions outlive implementations. Frameworks and libraries change; the business reasoning behind a modular, removable design does not.
  • New contributors get the context. An ADR gives a reader the reasoning behind the wiring, so they can tell when a change would contradict an accepted decision.
  • Review has a reference. A pull request that quietly reverses an accepted decision is visible the moment it contradicts an ADR.

items.title: Keep decisions business-focused
items.text:
An ADR records a decision that constrains or enables business capabilities. Implementation detail — how a library is configured, which version of a framework is pinned — belongs in code and project documentation, not here.

The litmus test

Would this decision still matter if we replaced every technology in the stack? If yes, it is an ADR. If no, it is an implementation detail.

ADR material Not ADR material One shared domain model serves streaming and storage How pydantic-avro serialises a record Modules must be removable as whole slices Nx plugin configuration Real secrets are encrypted per project; only dev defaults are committed SOPS command-line flags Development infrastructure starts with the app that needs it Docker Compose syntax Every project documents itself; no central catalogues Zensical navigation entries

Write the Context as a business situation (cost, risk, time-to-market, team autonomy, compliance), not as a technology comparison. Technologies may appear as evidence, but the drivers must stand without them.

State the Decision as a property that now holds, and name the current implementation only under Neutral / follow-ups. A record titled with a technology goes stale when the technology is replaced; a record titled with a property survives the replacement and says what replaced it.

items.title: Lifecycle
items.text:
• Number records NNN-short-slug (e.g. 001-single-monorepo.md); numbers are never reused.
  • Statuses: Proposed → Accepted, then optionally Superseded (by a later record) or Deprecated.
Proposed or Accepted — what exactly is the test?

Where the mechanism lives, not how uniformly it is used. Accepted means the decision is made and the mechanism that makes it true exists in the spine of the system; a part that skips an existing mechanism is a named deviation in the record's follow-ups, which does not by itself block acceptance. Proposed means the decision is not yet made, or the mechanism does not yet exist where it must. A stated convention the parts follow is itself an enforcement point: the record is Accepted and a missing automated check is a named gap, not a Proposed status.

  • Never edit the decision of an accepted record. When the business situation changes, write a new record that supersedes it and update the old record's status line only.
  • When a record is superseded, check the records that cite it: a requirement borrowed from a superseded record no longer has a foundation, so the dependent record either adopts the requirement in its own words, cites the superseding record, or is itself revisited — recorded in a new record, not by editing the old decision.
  • Add each new record to the nav section of mkdocs.yaml.

items.title: Using ADRs
items.text:
• Start the log at 001 and keep the numbering consecutive; the log belongs to whoever maintains the codebase.
  • State every requirement in the record's own words. A requirement phrased as "the property NNN demands" outsources its foundation to another record: if that record is superseded, the requirement loses its reason for existing — the same failure the supersession rule above guards against, from the drafting side.
  • Reference the records that govern an area in pull requests touching it and link to them from the project documentation they explain.
  • Review them occasionally: a record whose consequences no longer hold is a signal to write its successor.

items.title: Terms used in these records
items.text:
The records use a small vocabulary consistently; these notes are the shared definitions.

  • Spine — the parts of the codebase that stay no matter which optional capabilities are removed: the example apps, shared libraries, and the development infrastructure (002). In this repository the catalogue's own server, dashboard, and search store form the spine — a named deviation recorded by 050.
  • Slice — an optional capability and the infrastructure it owns, removed as one unit (002).
  • The gate — the shared rule set that runs at commit time and in the pipeline (014).
  • Event platform — the message system business events flow through (005); where a record speaks of a stream, it means one of the platform's topics, named by 032 and guaranteed per 027. The slice was removed by 050; the term appears only in the records written for that slice.
  • Collection point — the single seam where parts hand over traces, metrics, and logs (016).
  • Taught path — the arrangement an example demonstrates, which a future reader copies (009).
  • Delivery plane — the pipeline activity that validates and releases the system, distinct from the running system; the only place the data boundary may be crossed, and only at named points (036).
  • Dataset owner — the named role that answers for a dataset's shape, lifetime, and quality (042).
  • Swept (date tag) — a note in a record's status block that its wording passed the plain-language readability sweep on that date (the rules of the writing style guide); the tag touches wording only, never the decision, status, or trigger lines.

items.title: Gaps with a record but no mechanism yet
items.text:
Some questions the records lean on were listed here when they had no record at all. Each now has one, Proposed: the question is framed, the requirements are written, and the decision — including the numbers and owners those records defer — is what acceptance adds.

Which records are Proposed

Eight: 023, 025, 026, 027 (its slice removed by 050), 038, 040, 042, and 052 — the governance mechanisms that need an enforcement point before they are decisions the system keeps; 052's harness arrives with increment 0.4. Each is listed in the log above as Proposed.

The gaps also sequence the work: taking on real stored data needs the migration path (023) and the recovery path (026) first.

  • Storage schema lifecycle — 023, which 004 and 017 were assumed to lean on.
  • Data retention — 025, inside the boundary 016 draws.
  • Recovery — 026.
  • Event delivery guarantees — 027, the behaviour beside the content that 017 does not cover. The slice it governs was removed by 050; the record stays open in case a queue returns.
  • Authorization — 038, the permission question the identity record (007) deliberately leaves open.
  • Alerting — 040, the noticing the collection point (034) does not do by itself.
  • Dataset ownership — 042, the answer the migration path (023) and the lifetimes (025) each need someone to give.

A gap is listed here only while its record is Proposed. Accepting a record moves its status into the log above; finding a new gap means writing a record for it, not editing the records above.

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
• Copy the ADR Template when writing a record.
  • This section sits alongside the governance pages under Architecture: those describe target-state capabilities, ADRs record the decisions that shaped them.

items.title: 001. Keep one monorepo for every stack
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-06
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

All first-party work — every language, application, library, and piece of development infrastructure — lives in one repository run by one task runner, so a cross-stack change is a single atomic commit. Modules leave as whole slices; the repository itself never splits.
path: 001. Keep one monorepo for every stack

items.title: Decision
items.text:
One repository, one task runner. The runner understands each toolchain natively, so build, test, and run have one entry point everywhere.

A change that crosses a technology boundary must remain possible as a single reviewable, atomic commit. Modules may be removed wholesale (002); the organisation will not split what remains into separate repositories.
path: 001. Keep one monorepo for every stack

items.title: Context
items.text:
The organisation delivers one business system across several stacks — interface, backend services, shared libraries, and the infrastructure that runs them — and its capabilities only pay off end to end: a shared business concept, a customer or an order, is realised from the screen through the services into storage.

The business situation:

  • One multi-disciplinary team delivers work, so a single feature routinely touches several technologies at once.
  • The team is small: everyone shares the libraries, workflow, and docs; nobody owns a single technology.
  • New joiners must understand how the pieces fit, not bootstrap a setup.
  • Releases follow business milestones, so a shared-concept change lands everywhere at once.

The decision is how many sources of truth the delivery path has — one place where code and workflow live, or several. The cost of getting it wrong is paid for years afterwards, in every review spanning a boundary and every release needing coordination — by the people making the changes, not by whoever chose the layout.
path: 001. Keep one monorepo for every stack

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable layout must deliver:

Requirement R1 Atomic cross-stack change. A shared-concept change ships as one unit, no coordinated releases. R2 One way to run the system. One entry point for build/test/run, learned once by onboarding and CI. R3 Coherence at small-team cost. Shared code, workflow, and docs stay consistent as they evolve. R4 One place to learn the system. A new developer browses the whole system in one place. R5 Ownership matches staffing. Boundaries reflect one multi-disciplinary group, not imaginary teams.
path: 001. Keep one monorepo for every stack

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Repository per technology (polyrepo) R1: a shared-concept change becomes multi-repo release coordination with windows where parts disagree. R3: workflow and docs duplicated per repo. R4: a joiner inherits repos plus the wiring between them. Folders with no unifying task runner R2: "run the whole system" has no answer — the everyday question for a joiner or CI. R3: every toolchain's workflow re-invented, re-maintained. Do nothing (each technology keeps its own repo) R1, R3 by default: shared code and docs drift between the parts; a joiner receives pieces, not a working whole.
path: 001. Keep one monorepo for every stack

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 001. Keep one monorepo for every stack

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• Cross-stack changes are atomic and reviewed once (R1).
  • The workflow is defined once and applies everywhere (R2, R3).
  • A new developer follows one business concept end to end without leaving the repository (R4).
path: 001. Keep one monorepo for every stack

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• The repository carries tooling for several ecosystems, and every toolchain decision must coexist with the others.
  • Checkout and CI cost grows with everything included.
  • No repository-level access boundary: module discipline is a convention, not a wall.
path: 001. Keep one monorepo for every stack

items.title: Watch
items.text:
What stops the monorepo from rotting?

Two compensating rules, each with its own record: modules removable as whole slices (002) and documentation colocated with what it documents (003). The wall is not enforced by repository boundaries, so these conventions are the enforcement.
path: 001. Keep one monorepo for every stack

items.title: 002. Modules are removable as whole slices
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-06
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Every module is spine (always stays) or an optional capability that leaves as a whole slice: delete its directories and the remainder works. Partial removal is not a supported state — a team takes a capability in full, or not at all.
path: 002. Modules are removable as whole slices

items.title: Decision
items.text:
Two categories, no third. A module is part of the spine — the core that stays in every copy of this system — or it belongs to an optional capability.

A capability owns its applications, libraries, and development infrastructure together. Deleting it — code, wiring, configuration, documentation in one pass — leaves the remainder working. A team takes a capability in full or does not take it at all.

What is the spine today?

The spine is listed in the root AGENTS.md: the server, dashboard, store, parity, and trace projects, the dev infrastructure, and the template's example apps — which stay in the spine until increment 6.4 retires them as their own slice (DD-019). The template's Kafka streaming and AWS Lambda slices and its Java tooling were the first capabilities to leave this way (050).
path: 002. Modules are removable as whole slices

items.title: Context
items.text:
The repository holds a complete business system, built by one team, with nothing being removed today. It is also meant to be read and reused as a whole — the reason it lives in one repository (001) — and work taken from it takes a subset: a form-driven service has no use for a streaming pipeline; a serverless team's infrastructure needs differ from a long-lived-services team's.

The tension: the more capabilities the system demonstrates, the more useful it is as a reference — and the more a reader must sift to find their part.

Without a rule about how the system may be taken apart, two failure modes are open:

  • Removal by archaeology. Someone dropping a capability discovers by trial and error which libraries, wiring, keys, and documents belong to it — and usually leaves some behind.
  • Threading. A capability added with no rule has no reason to stay separable, so it threads a dependency through something general-purpose.

Either way the repository accumulates parts that belong to no one, and the cost of understanding it rises for everyone who reads it.
path: 002. Modules are removable as whole slices

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 Complete removal by deletion. Delete the capability's directories; no hunting for hidden wiring. R2 The remainder still works. What remains builds, tests, and runs without reference to what was deleted. R3 Wiring is not interleaved. Removal is deletion, not an editing task on files someone else owns. R4 Cheap to take back. Adding a capability later needs no rework of what exists. R5 Cheap to keep true. The rule holds with a small team, no dedicated owner per capability.
path: 002. Modules are removable as whole slices

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Free-form composition (any module, any dep) R1, R2: no boundary at which a capability ends, so removal is a hunt through shared files. R3 outright: one capability's wiring runs through files the whole system shares. Fine-grained modules, one per component R5: keeping a graph of small modules coherent is ongoing work a small team cannot fund. R1 degrades: "which parts form the streaming capability?" stops having one answer. Fork per capability combination R2 in the direction that matters: the fork diverges, fixes stop flowing. R4: taking an improvement back is a rework of everything the fork changed. Do nothing (document nothing about removal) R1, R2 by default: the first remover discovers boundaries by breaking the build, and writes down nothing for the next one.
path: 002. Modules are removable as whole slices

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 002. Modules are removable as whole slices

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• A capability is taken or dropped as a unit — the system serves teams that need only part (R1, R2).
  • Ownership is legible: everything belonging to a capability sits together (R3).
  • The rule asks for colocated wiring, not new machinery (R5).
path: 002. Modules are removable as whole slices

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• Capabilities cannot share infrastructure freely: where two rely on one backing service, one must own it — and removing that owner strands the other.
  • Some general-purpose work is duplicated rather than shared, because sharing would cut a capability in half.
  • Every addition is classified core-or-optional, a judgement occasionally re-litigated.
path: 002. Modules are removable as whole slices

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• Nothing in the build enforces the boundaries: the rule holds because the repository makes each capability's parts easy to see — which depends on every project documenting itself (003).
  • Infrastructure shared by several capabilities is owned by the capability whose directory holds it, stated in that capability's own documentation, where a remover reads it.
  • A part belongs to its capability by sitting in its directories and being listed in its documentation; a part that is neither is invisible to a removal sweep — a defect in that documentation, not bad luck.
path: 002. Modules are removable as whole slices

items.title: 003. Every project documents itself
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-06
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Knowledge lives beside the thing it describes: every project carries its own documentation, and the repository maintains no hand-edited central catalogue. The tree is the index.

items.title: Decision
items.text:
Documentation travels with its subject. Every project carries its own — what it is, how to run it, the rules that govern it — and the repository maintains no hand-edited central catalogue of projects or capabilities.

The repository tree is the index: to find what exists, read the tree; to learn a part, read what sits beside it. Derived artifacts — generated API reference, navigation derived from the tree — are not catalogues in the sense this rule forbids, because they cannot disagree with the code.

Isn't the site's nav list a central catalogue?

It is the one hand-edited list this rule tolerates. It enumerates documents rather than describing projects, and the build reports every entry that no longer resolves and every document the list omits — drift is loud at build time, not quiet at read time. That is the property R2 asks of everything else.

items.title: Context
items.text:
People constantly need to learn parts they did not build: what a part is for, how to run it, what breaks if it is removed. The team is small and multi-disciplinary, and the person who changes a project today is often not the person who needs to understand it next — so what the system does cannot live in anyone's head.

Where documentation lives decides how fast it decays:

  • Central knowledge changes only when someone remembers to update it, drifts from the code, and readers learn to distrust it.
  • Knowledge beside the code changes in the same review, is reviewed with it, and is deleted with it.

The decision is where knowledge about a part belongs, and what must be updated when that part changes.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 Knowledge travels with the part. Project and documentation change in the same review. R2 Drift is structurally impossible. No hand-edited central artifact quietly goes stale. R3 Local discovery is enough. Learn a part without leaving it. R4 Removal takes the knowledge with it. Deleting a project deletes its documentation. R5 Cheap to keep true. Honouring the rule costs nothing beyond the change already being made.

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails A curated catalogue of every project R2: a hand-edited page is updated when someone remembers — precisely how catalogues come to be disbelieved. R1: every change is a two-place edit in two reviews. R3: answering about a part means leaving it. The project wiki R1: edited by whoever remembers, reviewed apart from the change, so it drifts. R3: the answer lives elsewhere. R4: deleting a project leaves its page standing. No rule (knowledge in people and history) R3 by default: every question about an unfamiliar part becomes a question to a person. R1: nothing connects what changed to any written account. Documentation generated from code only R2 holds trivially — derived text cannot drift. R1 fails: code states what a project does, not why it is shaped that way; the reasoning must be written by a person, somewhere.

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• Documentation is reviewed with the change it describes — current exactly where people work (R1).
  • Drift is not discouraged but impossible: there is nothing central to forget (R2).
  • Removal leaves no stale text (R4) — what makes whole-slice removal trustworthy (002).

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• No single page answers "what does the system contain?" — discovery means browsing the tree, slower for a newcomer who doesn't yet know what to look for.
  • The shape of a project's documentation is a convention: keeping twenty documents consistent without an enforcing tool takes deliberate effort.

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• "Documents itself" needs a shared shape — what every project's documentation must contain — or the rule degrades into twenty unrelated files. Directory-level recipes for adding new projects carry that shape; keeping them current is ongoing work.
  • The removal rule in 002 depends on this record: a capability is fully removable only when its documentation is part of the slice.

items.title: 004. One shared domain model serves streaming and storage
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-06
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Each shared business concept has exactly one canonical definition, held outside any technology. Copies elsewhere are generated from it where generation is possible and checked against it where it isn't — a copy that is neither is a violation, not a tolerated variant.
path: 004. One shared domain model serves streaming and storage

items.title: Decision
items.text:
One canonical definition per concept, held outside any single technology. Representations of the concept elsewhere are generated from it where generation is possible and checked against it where it is not.

The same definition serves the concept in motion and at rest: one statement of what an order is governs the records that stream between systems and the rows that persist in storage. Changing the concept is one change, and its consequences are visible everywhere at once.
path: 004. One shared domain model serves streaming and storage

items.title: Context
items.text:
The business system moves the same concepts across boundaries — entered on a screen, processed by a service, streamed between services, persisted in a database. Each place speaks its technology's dialect, and left to itself each keeps its own description of the concept.

The cost falls due at every boundary. When two places describe one concept differently, someone translates between them, and translation code is where meaning is quietly lost: a field dropped, a meaning shifted, a field added in one place and unknown in another. These surface as data-integrity incidents and integration work — months after the change that caused them, owned by whoever is nearest the symptom.

A concept also has to survive transport between systems not built together, so its description must be legible to receivers that do not share the producing codebase.

The decision is where a shared concept's definition lives, and how its copies are kept honest.
path: 004. One shared domain model serves streaming and storage

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 One concept, one definition. One authoritative statement per concept, owned by no single consumer. R2 Drift is detected, not discovered. A mismatch fails a build or test — not a customer, later. R3 One definition in motion and at rest. A record in motion and a row at rest cannot mean different things. R4 Change is one edit. Evolving a concept is a single change whose full impact is visible in one review. R5 Portable across boundaries. Consumable by systems outside the codebase without sharing code.
path: 004. One shared domain model serves streaming and storage

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Per-stack models with mapping layers R1: as many definitions as stacks. R2 structurally: a mapping layer absorbs drift rather than detecting it, so divergence becomes a runtime difference. R4: one coordinated edit per stack, per change. The storage schema as the contract R2 for what matters most: a schema constrains rows, not records in motion, so streaming consumers evolve against a contract they never consult. R5: binds a business concept to one storage technology. Per-consumer schemas, negotiated at integration R1 immediately: the concept is defined once per integration. R2: nothing checks that two negotiated formats still describe one concept a year later. Do nothing (each stack keeps its own model) R2 by default: drift is found by whoever notices the data disagreeing. R4 by default: every concept change is N edits in N reviews by N people.
path: 004. One shared domain model serves streaming and storage

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 004. One shared domain model serves streaming and storage

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• A concept change is one reviewed change with visible blast radius (R4).
  • Representations cannot silently disagree: the generable ones are generated, the rest are checked (R2).
  • The concept travels outside the organisation as a plain artifact, not a library in a company language (R5).
path: 004. One shared domain model serves streaming and storage

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• The canonical definition becomes a shared dependency: changing it touches every consumer, so concept changes need an evolution policy (what may be added, what breaks consumers) that per-stack models never had to write down.
  • Some consumers need only a projection of a concept, and hand-maintaining that projection is exactly the copy this record exists to eliminate.
path: 004. One shared domain model serves streaming and storage

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• Representations that can't be generated today — a hand-written model in a dynamic language, a type in the interface, an inline schema in a flow tool — are kept in step by convention until a check exists. Under this record that is a gap to close, not a tolerated state: a representation found out of step is regenerated, not reconciled by hand.

Convention is a gap, not a state

The sentence above is the record's sharpest edge: a hand-written copy that no check verifies is drift waiting to happen, and the record refuses to accept it as normal. The closing mechanism is interface verification (030) — until a check exists, treat every unverified copy as a to-do with a due date.

  • For interfaces between parts, the verification rule (030) takes it up — a representation nobody checks against is where drift starts.
path: 004. One shared domain model serves streaming and storage

items.title: 005. Development infrastructure starts with the app that needs it
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-06
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

An application's development infrastructure starts when the application runs and stops with the run. No always-on shared environment; no app depends on infrastructure someone else started. One command, from fresh checkout to working system.
path: 005. Development infrastructure starts with the app that needs it

items.title: Decision
items.text:
The run brings its own infrastructure. An application's database, identity provider, event platform, and observability backends start when the application is run and stop with that run. No application depends on infrastructure somebody else started.

The run command is the entry point: it brings up the services the application declares, then the application. From a fresh checkout, one command per application is enough to see the system work.

This record settles who owns development infrastructure and when it exists; which machine the whole system runs on is decided separately (006).

Two apps need the same Keycloak — do I start it twice?

Per run, yes. The isolation is the point: a shared always-on provider is the named alternative, and it fails on shared state — one person's sign-in changes another's results. The cost is real (the provider starts per run) and bought deliberately; a run's infrastructure is declared by the app that uses it and dies with the run.
path: 005. Development infrastructure starts with the app that needs it

items.title: Context
items.text:
The system is several small applications, each depending on services — a database, an identity provider, metrics — so every developer faces the same question before feature work: how do I get a running system in front of me? Two conventional answers, both with costs:

  • A shared always-on environment: front-loads the work with access requests and setup instructions, and shares state — what one person changes is visible in everyone else's results.
  • A documented manual setup: puts the system in front of the developer only as reliably as the list is current, and lists go stale without anyone noticing.

Both share a slower cost: the cost of trying the system decides how often it is run, and a system that is rarely run is rarely observed. Where the codebase's examples are its demonstration, an example nobody runs is an example nobody can vouch for.
path: 005. Development infrastructure starts with the app that needs it

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 One command to a running system. From a fresh checkout; no manual prerequisite steps. R2 Runs do not interfere. Two apps, or two developers, at once — one run cannot change another's results. R3 Dependencies declared where used. In the application's own definition, so the list travels with it. R4 Reproducible everywhere. New developer, fresh machine, CI — same command, no knowledge held by whoever set up last. R5 Nothing accumulates. The run ends, its infrastructure ends; no state between runs. R6 Cheap to keep true. Changing dependencies is a local edit by the person making the change.
path: 005. Development infrastructure starts with the app that needs it

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Shared always-on development environment R2 structurally: shared state, one person's run changes everyone's results, debugging becomes "who else is connected?" R5: outlives every run, accumulates state nobody owns. R1 at the front door: access provisioning is a prerequisite. One root compose file that starts the whole world R3: what starts is the full list, not what one app uses, so list and reality drift. R6: adding an app is an edit to a global file. A documented manual setup R1: the list is the prerequisite. R4: works on the machine of whoever last wrote it down, nowhere else. Do nothing (each developer wires their own stack) R1 by default: every run is bespoke. R2 by default: every stack differs slightly, every mismatch debugged as an app bug.
path: 005. Development infrastructure starts with the app that needs it

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 005. Development infrastructure starts with the app that needs it

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• Clone-to-running is one command, no prerequisites (R1).
  • Runs are isolated: a broken run is the developer's own to fix (R2).
  • The dependency list lives with the application — removing a module removes its infrastructure (R3).
  • New developer, colleague, and CI all take the same path (R4).
  • Changing what an app needs is a local edit (R6).
path: 005. Development infrastructure starts with the app that needs it

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• Startup cost is paid per run, not amortised over a shared environment: bring-up must stay fast — images kept current, services started in parallel.
  • Several applications running at once means several stacks whose ports and resource use must be coordinated.
path: 005. Development infrastructure starts with the app that needs it

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• Every application needs a run command that brings up its declared infrastructure; an app whose run target is a build tool or emulator deviates from this record until it has one.
  • The convention keeping parallel stacks from colliding on ports is a convention, not a check — and remains so until a collision has happened once.
path: 005. Development infrastructure starts with the app that needs it

items.title: 006. The whole system runs on one machine
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-06
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Every application, service, and dependency runs on the machine of the person doing the work — brought up by automation, the same arrangement the pipeline validates on every change. The rule constrains what may enter: a dependency that exists only as a hosted service needs a local equivalent first.
path: 006. The whole system runs on one machine

items.title: Decision
items.text:
One machine holds the whole system. The machine of the person doing the work runs every application, every service, and the infrastructure between them, brought up by automation rather than by procedure.

The pipeline validates the same arrangement. What the pipeline proves on every change is what a person can bring up on demand — a green pipeline and a working local run are claims about the same thing.

The rule constrains what may enter, not just where it runs. A dependency that exists only as a service elsewhere needs a local equivalent before the system may depend on it.
path: 006. The whole system runs on one machine

items.title: Context
items.text:
The system's behaviour lives in the interactions between parts, not inside any one part, so defects surface wherever the whole system runs.
