Two candidates: infrastructure the organisation operates (scale, realism) and the engineer's machine (the whole system in front of the person who must understand it).

What either place is worth depends on how often the system runs there, and frequency follows cost. Validation that is expensive to run happens rarely; validation that happens rarely lags the code it should validate — the gap is found later, by someone else, at higher cost.

One machine sounds like a toy — why is it a requirement?

It is not a claim about scale; production runs where the deployment puts it. The requirement is about frequency: the whole system must run in front of the person changing it, on every change, so the pipeline's green and the laptop's run are claims about the same arrangement. The rule spends its force on admission: a hosted-only dependency needs a local equivalent first.
path: 006. The whole system runs on one machine

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 The investigator reproduces the defect. Whole, quickly, repeatably — no operated infrastructure to keep available. R2 Validation covers the parts working together. Every change, unattended — not part by part, not waiting for a person. R3 Work needs no operated infrastructure. No reachable services, no network, no provisioned accounts. R4 Running it is an everyday act. Bring-up, work, teardown in minutes. Hours means the premise has failed. R5 Cheap to keep true. Adding a service is a local edit to the environment definition, not a change request.
path: 006. The whole system runs on one machine

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Organisation-operated development environment R1: reproducing means investigating through the platform — its state, availability, access. R4: the everyday loop queues behind shared infrastructure. Apps local, infrastructure cloud-hosted R3 outright: every loop reaches services its owner doesn't control, needs network and accounts. R1: reproduce against someone else's services. One orchestration everywhere R3: the organisation now operates a platform beside the system. R4: the loop waits on a cluster one app doesn't need. R5: adding a service changes cluster definitions. Validation in the pipeline only R1: a failure nobody can reproduce off-platform is a second-class defect, debuggable only by platform-access holders. Do nothing (parts run wherever they happen to) R2 by default: the system runs as a whole nowhere until someone assembles it by hand. R4: every run is a planned assembly; every machine accumulates its own environment.
path: 006. The whole system runs on one machine

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 006. The whole system runs on one machine

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• A production incident reproduces on a laptop, no access provisioning.
  • Everyday work runs offline, with no accounts and no access requests.
  • The pipeline and the local run prove the same arrangement — no translation gap.
path: 006. The whole system runs on one machine

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• The rule constrains what may enter: every part must be startable by automation on one machine, so a hosted-only dependency needs a local stand-in — and every stand-in is a maintained artifact (012).
  • Validating the full stack unattended costs real minutes and real money per run.
  • Confidence stops at the environment boundary; 010 names its exceptions.
path: 006. The whole system runs on one machine

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• Every application needs a run target that brings up what a run needs — the obligation 005 places on each app.
  • The cost of validating on every change is bounded by validating the parts a change can reach, with the full arrangement reserved for unbounded reach — where that line sits is a pipeline decision this record does not make.
path: 006. The whole system runs on one machine

items.title: 007. One shared identity provider serves every authenticated surface
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-06
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

People exist in exactly one place: a shared identity provider. Every surface that authenticates a human delegates to it — no surface holds accounts, credentials, or a sign-in flow. The provider runs wherever the system runs, so the authenticated path is exercised everywhere the system is validated.
path: 007. One shared identity provider serves every authenticated surface

items.title: Decision
items.text:
The provider is the only place people exist. Every surface that authenticates a human — screens, the APIs behind them, operational tooling — delegates: the provider decides who a person is and whether they are admitted now; surfaces act only on what the provider has issued.

Surfaces stay thin: no user accounts, no stored credentials, no sign-in flow — they verify tokens against the provider.

The provider is part of the system, not a service beside it: it runs on an engineer's machine and in the pipeline, so the authenticated path is exercised everywhere the system is validated (006).
path: 007. One shared identity provider serves every authenticated surface

items.title: Context
items.text:
People touch the system in several places — the screens where work is entered, the APIs behind them, the tooling that operates it. Each must know who is acting, and left to itself each keeps its own list of people.

  • People join, change roles, and leave. When a person leaves, the business must stop recognising them everywhere at once. With identity per surface, revocation is a checklist whose completeness depends on whoever carries it out.
  • Access is audited. The auditor asks who could reach what, and when. One place answers directly; several places require reconciling records by hand.
  • Admission is code that has to run to be trusted. A sign-in path that only exists in production is a path no earlier run has exercised — and identity code carries the least tolerance for unexercised paths.
Why not per-app auth?

Each bullet above is the answer: leaving a person is a checklist across surfaces, an audit becomes reconciliation by hand, and every app's sign-in flow is identity code that runs only in production. One provider exercised everywhere the system is validated replaces all three with one path that is never unexercised.

The decision is where "who is this person, and are they in?" lives, and who may answer it.
path: 007. One shared identity provider serves every authenticated surface

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 One answer about people. One authoritative statement of who is admitted; no surface keeps its own list. R2 Revocation is one action. Ending access at the provider ends it everywhere, on the next request — not the next release. R3 Surfaces stay thin. No credentials stored, no tokens issued, no sign-in flow. Security code is written, reviewed, patched once. R4 Identity runs where validation runs. The provider runs locally and in CI (006), so authenticated paths are exercised in every validation. R5 The provider is replaceable. Surfaces integrate through a standard interface.
path: 007. One shared identity provider serves every authenticated surface

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Per-surface identity R1: as many answers about people as surfaces. R2: revocation is a tour of every surface, complete when someone remembers every stop. R3: every surface writes its own password and session handling — every one a breach site. The cloud platform's identity service R4: the everyday loop and every unattended run reach a service behind a cloud account and a network — the authenticated path can't run offline (006). A home-grown auth service R5: the interface is whatever the first surface needed, so replacing it is a rewrite; the credential code is permanently the organisation's own audit surface. Do nothing (surfaces unauthenticated until needed) R1 by default: the first surface needing auth invents what the next inherits. R4: admission is exercised for the first time in production — where identity bugs are least affordable.
path: 007. One shared identity provider serves every authenticated surface

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 007. One shared identity provider serves every authenticated surface

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• Revocation is one action with immediate effect (R2).
  • Credential and session code exists once, reviewed once, patched once (R3).
  • The authenticated path runs on every machine and pipeline: auth regressions fail a build, not a user (R4).
  • Surfaces speak a standard interface — the provider is replaceable (R5).
path: 007. One shared identity provider serves every authenticated surface

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• The provider is critical infrastructure: while it is down, every authenticated surface is down — it is the business system's front door.
  • The local environment carries one more service to start, version, and keep current.
  • Identity is where compliance looks hardest: where the provider stores user data, and who administers it, is constrained by policy, not preference.
path: 007. One shared identity provider serves every authenticated surface

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The current implementation is a self-hosted provider speaking OIDC, with the application registered as a public client in a realm of its own.
  • This record covers people only. Services that move data and calls between surfaces — streaming paths, service-to-service calls — are not people: their identity is a separate decision (013).
path: 007. One shared identity provider serves every authenticated surface

items.title: 008. Real secrets are encrypted; only dev defaults are committed
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-06
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Real secrets exist in the codebase only as ciphertext, encrypted to a named recipient list; plaintext files carry dev defaults only. The recipient list is the access list — changing it is an edit, not a hunt.
path: 008. Real secrets are encrypted; only dev defaults are committed

items.title: Decision
items.text:
Plaintext never carries a real secret. A secret the system needs is encrypted to a named set of recipients and committed as ciphertext; what the codebase carries in plaintext is dev defaults — values safe to publish.

Access is the recipient list. Who can read the secrets is exactly that list; changing the set of readers is an edit to it.

Reading and writing is part of running, not a side trip. Bring-up decrypts what a run needs (005); the loop never waits on a secret store (006). The ciphertext travels with the code, so cloning, forking, and caching are safe acts.
path: 008. Real secrets are encrypted; only dev defaults are committed

items.title: Context
items.text:
The system runs on secrets — database passwords, service tokens, signing keys — and between creation and use a secret rests somewhere. Where it rests, and who can read it there, is the decision.

  • The codebase's history is permanent and endlessly copied. A committed file reaches everyone who ever clones, every pipeline cache, every fork, and is recalled from none of them. A real secret committed in plaintext is not a mistake to correct but a breach to remediate: rotate every credential, audit the exposure.
  • The readers are a small, named set — the people who build and operate the system. So "who can read this secret?" is answered explicitly, by encrypting to named recipients, not implicitly by whoever holds a copy.
path: 008. Real secrets are encrypted; only dev defaults are committed

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 History never carries plaintext. A real secret enters as ciphertext; plaintext is never the default path. R2 The loop never waits on a secret service. A full local run, no live store — no dependency re-entered side doors. R3 Access is a list, not a trail. One explicit set; removing a person ends future access by editing the set. R4 One mechanism everywhere. Machine, pipeline, deployment — no environment invents its own handling. R5 Cheap to keep true. Adding a secret or a person is a small edit, not a standing project.
path: 008. Real secrets are encrypted; only dev defaults are committed

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Cloud secret manager, nothing in the repository R2: every loop and unattended run reaches a service behind a cloud account — the system stops being runnable offline (006). R4: the local loop needs a fallback, and the fallback is a plaintext file. A vault per environment R2 for the same reason. R4: the loop starts and configures a vault. R5: standing up, versioning, administering vaults is a standing project. Trust the ignore list R1: an ignore list is a wish, not a wall — one forced add, one renamed file, one tool committing what it was given, and the breach is permanent. R3: "who can read this" becomes "everyone who ever held a copy." Do nothing (secrets handled as they come) R1 by default: every password pasted into config or chat is a future remediation. R3 by default: access is whatever the copies say.
path: 008. Real secrets are encrypted; only dev defaults are committed

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 008. Real secrets are encrypted; only dev defaults are committed

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• The codebase can be cloned, forked, mirrored, cached — none of those acts is a breach (R1).
  • Development stays fully offline-capable (R2).
  • Who can read secrets is one list; revoking a person is an edit to it (R3).
  • One mechanism serves machine, pipeline, and deployment (R4).
path: 008. Real secrets are encrypted; only dev defaults are committed

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• The decryption key becomes the crown jewels: losing it locks the organisation out of its own secrets, leaking it decrypts the whole history. Key custody is a business process with named owners.
  • Adding or removing a person re-encrypts every secret file — rotation is cheap but never free.
  • The rule protects history only from the day it starts: secrets committed before it are still exposed and still need rotation.
path: 008. Real secrets are encrypted; only dev defaults are committed

items.title: Watch
items.text:
Production rides the same mechanism — don't fight it

Production secrets are encrypted to a named set of people. Rotating a production credential quickly, or granting a break-glass reader, means touching that list; treating it as friction is how the mechanism gets bypassed. Operational secret handling beyond the list is the question 028 takes up.

  • Any plaintext configuration found carrying a real value moves into ciphertext rather than being argued about — which means the line between a dev default and a real secret needs a check that flags likely-real values before they reach history.
path: 008. Real secrets are encrypted; only dev defaults are committed

items.title: 009. Every example runs and is tested, or it is removed
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-06
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Every example is a working implementation, verified by tests the pipeline runs against real services. An example that can't hold that bar is removed, not annotated.
path: 009. Every example runs and is tested, or it is removed

items.title: Decision
items.text:
An example is a small implementation, held to the system's bar — it runs the way the rest of the system runs, and its behaviour is verified by tests in the pipeline. An example that cannot hold that standard is removed, not annotated.

Because the system runs everywhere it is validated (006), examples run there too: on an engineer's machine and in the pipeline, against real services, with their real behaviour tested.
path: 009. Every example runs and is tested, or it is removed

items.title: Context
items.text:
The codebase carries examples — a service wired to the database, a flow wired to the stream, a screen wired to the API. People read them and copy them, and a copied example becomes the standard for whatever is built next. The examples are how the codebase teaches, intended or not.

An example, unlike ordinary code, has no callers. Ordinary code that breaks breaks loudly: its dependents fail. An example depends on nothing, so when it stops working, nothing notices. Its health is whoever last ran it by hand — and the first person to discover the breakage is a reader who has already trusted it, often a new person, who cannot tell a deliberate simplification from rot.

The two errors cost differently:

  • Removing a good example costs a directory and a lost teaching artifact.
  • A broken example left in place teaches its mistake with the authority of the codebase, and the mistake can be copied before it is noticed.
Why remove a broken example, not fix it later?

"Later" is where the asymmetry above lives: every day in place, the broken example teaches with the codebase's authority, and the first reader to trust it is usually the newest. A fix-later promise has the same shape as the health the example already lost — someone ran it by hand, once. Removal is loud and dated; annotation is silent decay.
path: 009. Every example runs and is tested, or it is removed

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 The claim is tested, not remembered. A pipeline test, not "someone ran it once," backs the claim that it works. R2 Breakage fails a build, not a reader. Detected the day it breaks — not discovered by whoever trusts it. R3 The taught path is the shipped path. Real mechanisms, real services: a passing example means the path works. R4 Examples run like the rest. The same bring-up as the system (005, 006) — no special harness. R5 Removal is cheap. A local deletion that leaves nothing dangling.
path: 009. Every example runs and is tested, or it is removed

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Keep broken examples, annotated "for illustration" R1: the annotation is a claim no test runs, and rots like the code it labels. R2: nothing fails as the example drifts; a reader cannot tell illustration from rot. Documentation snippets instead of implementations R1: a snippet is never executed, so its correctness is a claim about the day it was written. R3: a quotation of the path, and quotations drift in silence. Examples tested against substitutes R3: the example demonstrates agreement with stubs, not the path that ships — and the integration failures the example exists to catch are exactly what stubs hide. Do nothing (examples live until someone complains) R1 by default: health is whoever last ran it by hand. R2 by default: breakage is discovered by readers — the one audience the arrangement exists to protect.
path: 009. Every example runs and is tested, or it is removed

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 009. Every example runs and is tested, or it is removed

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• What people copy is verified, against the real path, before they copy it (R1, R3).
  • An example that breaks fails a build the same day, and is never discovered by a reader months later (R2).
  • Examples double as the system's integration tests: teaching artifact and safety net are one code, maintained once.
path: 009. Every example runs and is tested, or it is removed

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• Every example is a maintained implementation — code, tests, services — so the honest response to an example falling behind is deletion. Cheap (R5), still a loss, and the honest consequence is that the set of examples stays small on purpose.
  • Real-service testing costs real pipeline minutes and money per run, more than substitutes (012).
path: 009. Every example runs and is tested, or it is removed

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The full chain — producer, stream, sink, service, screen — is proven segment by segment; a single test spanning all five is the test this record's own standard most wants.
  • 005 requires every application to have a run target; an example in an application that lacks one cannot yet be reached by the one-command path.
path: 009. Every example runs and is tested, or it is removed

items.title: 010. The unit validated is the unit that ships
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-06
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Every part ships as one packaged unit, and that same unit is what development and the pipeline validate. Environments differ in configuration and orchestration — never in artifact.
path: 010. The unit validated is the unit that ships

items.title: Decision
items.text:
One packaged unit per part. The unit built and validated on an engineer's machine and in the pipeline is the unit deployed to production. Environments may differ in configuration and in the orchestration that runs the unit — production runs on the orchestration the organisation operates, which need not be how the system runs in development or CI — but not in artifact.

A run is evidence about a unit; a deployment is of that unit. Where a difference between places is unavoidable, it is expressed as configuration of the unit, never as a differently built unit.
path: 010. The unit validated is the unit that ships

items.title: Context
items.text:
The system is validated in several places — an engineer's machine, the pipeline, production — and each validation produces a claim: the system behaves this way. The claims are worth acting on only if they are about the same thing.

If the validated artifact differs from the deployed artifact, a passing run and a healthy deployment are claims about two objects, and confidence does not transfer. The organisation is left reasoning about the gap: which failures belong to packaging, which to environment, which to code — a question that exists only because two builds happened where one could have.

What does a green run not prove?

The unit, not the environment: scale, live traffic, third-party behaviour, and the production orchestration itself are named exceptions this record refuses to claim. A passing run transfers its evidence about the artifact — configuration and orchestration differences are stated, not silently absorbed, and the gap is a list, not a fog.
path: 010. The unit validated is the unit that ships

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 One build, everywhere used. Packaged once per change; every consumer takes that package, never rebuilds. R2 Validation transfers to production. A passing run is evidence about what deploys — differences are config, not artifact. R3 The unit is self-contained. Carries what it needs to run; external dependencies are declared, not assumed from the machine. R4 Deploy is a selection, not a transformation. Point the environment at a validated unit — no rebuild, repackage, or patch on the way. R5 Cheap to keep true. Packaging a part is a local edit by the person making the change.
path: 010. The unit validated is the unit that ships

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Build per environment R1 by construction — the tested unit and the serving unit come from different builds at different times, every difference unvalidated. R4: deploying runs a build, so the release path contains a step no validation covered. Patch the validated unit at release R4 directly: the deployed unit is the validated unit plus an unvalidated edit, and the pipeline's claim ends where the edit begins. Deploy source, build in place R1: each environment's toolchain assembles its own copy — two environments, two running things, one commit. R4: the running thing has no identity to roll back to. Do nothing (each place takes what it takes) R1 by default: machine, pipeline, and production each assemble a copy. R2 by default: green here and green there are claims about different things; the gap is investigated when they disagree.
path: 010. The unit validated is the unit that ships

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 010. The unit validated is the unit that ships

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• A passing run means the same thing on a machine, in the pipeline, and in production (R1, R2).
  • Releasing is a selection, so rollback is a selection: point back at the previously validated unit (R4).
  • The running unit has an identity, so an incident ties to exactly the code that runs.
path: 010. The unit validated is the unit that ships

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• Every part must be packageable — arrangements that only work in place are out — and packaging joins every delivery path, so packaging bugs become release bugs.
  • Per-environment configuration must live outside the unit: a stated place for it, and the habit of keeping secrets and environment values out of the package.
path: 010. The unit validated is the unit that ships

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The confidence claim stops at the environment boundary: scale, live traffic, third-party behaviour, and the production orchestration itself are named exceptions, not proven by validating the unit.
  • Parts packaged non-uniformly (an app run from source, not its package) deviate from this record until they ship the unit that was tested.
  • The image developers and the pipeline work in is not a deliverable and not the unit this record governs: it is a tool for producing and validating the unit, and a change to it is not a release.
path: 010. The unit validated is the unit that ships

items.title: 011. The development environment is a versioned artifact
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-06
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

The environment developers and the pipeline run in is built from a definition in the repository. One base for every machine; machine differences stop at its boundary.
path: 011. The development environment is a versioned artifact

items.title: Decision
items.text:
The development environment is a versioned artifact, not a local arrangement. It is built from a definition in the repository, carries the toolchains, runtimes, and CLIs the work needs, and is the same on every machine — one base, not a variant per OS.

The definition is authoritative: a rebuild reproduces it, and a running instance carries no state the definition cannot reproduce. When the work needs a tool, the change is an edit to the definition, not a step performed on machines.
path: 011. The development environment is a versioned artifact

items.title: Context
items.text:
The tooling runs on machines the organisation does not fully control: laptops, CI runners, occasionally an engineer's workstation. The developer machine is the least controllable of these — people have their own machines, and each drifts: tools at assorted versions, paths assumed, utilities installed by accident. None of these is a decision, and the automation that runs against the estate discovers each difference, one at a time.

Left unmanaged, the automation adapts to the estate, spending effort on the estate instead of the system. The pipeline has no keyboard: it cannot do the machine preparation the tooling assumes. The difference between two machines becomes a difference the automation must carry.

The base image ships nothing — why govern it at all?

Because every claim the system makes is produced inside it. The base is the tool that produces and validates the shipped unit, not a deliverable and not the unit 010 governs — a change to it is not a release. What the record rules is its honesty: built from the definition, rebuilt on a stated trigger, one base for people and CI, so "works in the base" means works everywhere the work runs.
path: 011. The development environment is a versioned artifact

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 One base, people and pipelines. People and CI work in the same environment — a result in one is a result in the other. R2 Machine differences stop at the boundary. What a person's machine has, lacks, or is at some version stops affecting the work at the base. R3 Built, not inherited. Assembled from a definition in version control; reviewable with the change that needed a tool; rebuildable. R4 Unattended runs need no person. A clean machine runs the automation unattended; "set up your machine" is not a precondition. R5 A tool is a reviewed edit. Adding a tool changes the definition, reviewed with the change that asked for it.
path: 011. The development environment is a versioned artifact

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails A documented machine standard R2: a checklist covers what its author thought of; machines drift from it within weeks; the automation discovers the differences. R4: preparation is a person's task. A variant per operating system R1: the base is no longer one thing, and the automation carries the variants — conditionals per platform, multiplied across the estate. Rely on tools the machine already has R1: the base becomes the union of every machine's accidents; automation carries conditionals for machines that differ. R2/R3: nothing is declared; a clean machine has none of it. Do nothing (everyone sets up their own) R1 by default: every machine is its own environment, and "works on my machine" is a claim about one machine. R4 by default: unattended runs inherit whoever set the machine up.
path: 011. The development environment is a versioned artifact

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 011. The development environment is a versioned artifact

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• The automation is written once, against the base (R1).
  • Machine differences stop at the base (R2).
  • A clean machine runs the work with one command — which is what makes unattended CI and the offline laptop work (R3, R4).
  • A tool is added by a reviewed edit (R5).
path: 011. The development environment is a versioned artifact

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• The base is a maintained artifact; a stale base produces failures that look like application bugs.
  • The base sits in every delivery path: a base-build failure stops work for everyone, not one machine.
  • Tooling that cannot run in the base is excluded from the work — it needs a stated arrangement, not an ad-hoc one.
path: 011. The development environment is a versioned artifact

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The base is currently a container image; replacing the form changes the follow-through, not the rule. 010 governs the shipped unit, not the base.
  • Rebuild the base on a stated trigger: drift between the definition and a running environment is the difference this record exists to remove.
  • Where a part runs outside the base — the build tool, an emulator invoked directly — that part deviates.
  • The base is a tool for producing and validating the unit, not a deliverable: a change to the base is not a release (see 010).
path: 011. The development environment is a versioned artifact

items.title: 012. Validation runs against real services, not substitutes
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

The system's behaviour is validated against the real services it uses, brought up for the run and torn down after it. A test passing against a stub is evidence about the stub, not the system.
path: 012. Validation runs against real services, not substitutes

items.title: Decision
items.text:
Validation exercises the real services — the database, the identity provider, the event platform — brought up by the run and torn down after it. Substitutes (stubbed services, canned responses, hand-written fakes) are not the default path for validating behaviour.

A test that passes against a substitute is evidence about the substitute. Only a test that passes against the real thing is evidence about the system, and the organisation acts on the second kind.
path: 012. Validation runs against real services, not substitutes

items.title: Context
items.text:
The system is assembled from parts that talk to services: a service reads and writes storage, consumers move records through a stream, a front end calls an API that delegates admission to an identity provider. The failures that cost the business money live in those conversations — a driver that behaves differently than the client assumed, a constraint the code never expected, a handshake only the real service enforces.

Those conversations can be exercised against the real service or a stand-in. A stand-in starts faster and costs less per run, and carries a hidden cost:

  • It is a second implementation of the service's behaviour, written by people who only know the behaviour the code already assumes. Where the assumption is wrong, the stand-in agrees with it — the substitute hides precisely the failures the test exists to catch, silently and forever.
  • It is a second codebase, with its own bugs and its own upkeep — exactly the cost a small team cannot fund twice.

The decision is what behaviour is validated against, and what a passing test is allowed to be evidence of.
path: 012. Validation runs against real services, not substitutes

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 A passing test is evidence about the shipped path. The services a test exercises are production's, at the same interface. R2 Fidelity does not decay in silence. No hand-written model of a service's behaviour that can quietly disagree with it. R3 Runs need no accounts or network. The run brings the services up on the machine validating, so unattended and offline agree. R4 The cost stays bounded. Real minutes and real money per run, kept small enough that validation isn't rationed. R5 Cheap to keep true. Adding a validated part is a local edit, not work spread across a maintained fake world.
path: 012. Validation runs against real services, not substitutes

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Substitutes everywhere R2 structurally: a substitute is written from the code's own assumptions, so the two agree by construction and disagree with the service where nobody noticed. R1 for the same reason — the claim ends at the substitute's boundary. R5: the fake world must track every service it imitates. Recorded traffic replayed R1 on the day of capture, R2 afterwards: a recording is a claim about one day, the service evolves, and the replay agrees with old behaviour in silence. R4: recordings rot and must be re-captured — the substitute's upkeep with extra steps. Real services hosted by the platform R1 outright, R3 not at all: every run needs accounts, network, and a shared mutable service, so unattended runs wait on access someone provisioned and two runs contaminate each other. Do nothing (each test picks its level) R1 by default: a green suite becomes a mix of claims about the system and about substitutes, and no reader can tell which — so green stops meaning anything in particular.
path: 012. Validation runs against real services, not substitutes

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 012. Validation runs against real services, not substitutes

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• A passing test is evidence about the shipped path (R1): confidence transfers to production with no gap to reason about.
  • There is no fake world to build or maintain, which removes a whole category of silent disagreement (R2, R5).
  • Runs are self-contained, so the pipeline and an offline machine see the same result (R3).
path: 012. Validation runs against real services, not substitutes

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• Every run pays real startup and resource cost, so validation must stay targeted — the parts a change can reach — or the cost rations the testing.
  • Some services have no local equivalent at all; those runs wait on the exception rather than the rule.
path: 012. Validation runs against real services, not substitutes

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• A dependency that exists only as a hosted service is validated against a local equivalent, and drift between the two is a defect, not environment noise.
  • Each such dependency needs a named validation arrangement. Until it has one, it is a hole in R1 the organisation carries knowingly.
Why not stub the expensive services?

Because the expensive services are where the assumptions live. A stub encodes what the code already believes about the service, so it validates the belief instead of testing it — and the day the belief is wrong is the day the test goes green.
path: 012. Validation runs against real services, not substitutes

items.title: 013. Services prove who they are at every boundary
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Every call between two parts is authenticated in both directions: the credential says which service is calling, and an unauthenticated boundary is a defect, not a default. Machine identity is separate from human identity.
path: 013. Services prove who they are at every boundary

items.title: Decision
items.text:
Every boundary carries a verdict. Each call between two parts — a service to a database, one service to another — presents a credential the other side verifies; a rejected caller is turned away at the boundary, not trusted inside it.

Machine identity is separate from human identity. People are admitted by the shared identity provider (007); services by credentials issued to services. The rule is the same everywhere: the receiving side acts on what the credential says, not on which network the call arrived from.

Credentials are part of the system, not a service beside it. Issued, stored, and rotated by the arrangements the system already runs locally and in the pipeline, so the authenticated path is exercised wherever the system is validated.
path: 013. Services prove who they are at every boundary

items.title: Context
items.text:
The system is parts talking to parts, and each conversation crosses a boundary where one side decides whether to trust the other. When that decision is skipped, trust defaults to location: anything on the inside network is a colleague. That breaks in the ways that cost most:

  • Blast radius: a compromised part reaches everything its neighbours trusted.
  • Misconfiguration: a deployment joins a conversation it never belonged to.
  • Attribution: the audit trail says "something inside" acted, not which service — and for regulated data, "who moved this record" must name a service the way it names a person.

Services are not people: no password to remember, no interactive sign-in, created and destroyed by automation, credential arriving by the same path as configuration. Bolting human admission onto services ends with service credentials in people's hands or people's credentials embedded in services — one failure with two faces: the audit trail can no longer say who acted.

Machine identity and human identity — which is which?

Two questions with two answers: who is this person belongs to the shared provider (007), which service is calling belongs to credentials issued to services, verified at the boundary they arrive at. The line is what keeps a person's token out of a service and a service's key out of a laptop — and keeps "who acted" answerable in both registers.
path: 013. Services prove who they are at every boundary

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 Every boundary has a verdict. Both directions authenticated; a rejected caller is turned away at the boundary. R2 The audit trail names the caller. A record says which service acted, not which network it came from. R3 Machine identity is not human identity. Service credentials belong to services; revoking one touches no person. R4 Credentials travel with delivery. Same configuration path as everything else; a fresh deployment is authenticated without a person. R5 The authenticated path runs where validation runs. Local and unattended runs exercise it, not a more trusting variant. R6 Revocation is an edit. Retiring a service changes a stated set, not a hunt for copies of a shared value.
path: 013. Services prove who they are at every boundary

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Network location as identity R1: there is no verdict to make. R2: the trail records an address. R6: "revoking" means re-wiring reachability, and any second path revokes nothing. One shared secret for everything R1 thinly, R2 not at all — every caller looks identical. R6: revoking one caller means replacing the secret everywhere at once, which is never done. Human identity for services R3 by construction: the credential belongs to a person, so their departure revokes the service, and machine actions are attributed to them. Authenticate production only R5: the authenticated path exists only where identity failures are least affordable and least exercised — the same argument that puts human identity in every local run (007). Do nothing (boundaries close when remembered) R1 by default: every boundary is open and nobody knows which. R2 by default: unauthenticated conversations leave nothing to audit.
path: 013. Services prove who they are at every boundary

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 013. Services prove who they are at every boundary

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• A compromised part reaches only what its own credential allows (R1).
  • The trail names the calling service for machine actions as it names the person for human ones (R2).
  • Retiring a service is an edit to a stated set (R6); deployments are authenticated with no person in the loop (R4).
path: 013. Services prove who they are at every boundary

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• Every boundary gains a credential to issue, deliver, and rotate — real upkeep the open arrangement never paid.
  • Local and pipeline environments run the authenticated path too, so bring-up carries credential setup an open cluster avoids.
  • A wrong credential breaks a deployment loudly, where the open arrangement failed with no signal at all.
path: 013. Services prove who they are at every boundary

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The credential format per boundary (identity provider, platform, or deployment) is a follow-up per service, not settled here.
  • A service credential is a secret and rests where the secrets record says (008); who owns its rotation is the question a proposed record takes up (028).
path: 013. Services prove who they are at every boundary

items.title: Implementation
items.text:
Demonstrated, then removed with the slice. The rule was proven end-to-end on the development event platform, which at acceptance ran unauthenticated — a defect by this record's definition. The proof, before the slice left (050):

  • The local Kafka cluster was closed to anonymous callers: token callers arrive with OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens (SASL/OAUTHBEARER over TLS) from a dedicated kafka realm, each a distinct confidential client so the broker's session log names the caller (R1, R2, R3, R6).
  • Library exceptions arrive with per-service client certificates under mutual TLS.
  • Every E2E suite authenticates over TLS (R5).

The rule stands and now governs the boundaries the catalogue keeps: the server to its search store, its identity provider, and its HTTP API. Transport protection belongs to the data-protection record (039); this record covers the credential presented once the channel is open.
path: 013. Services prove who they are at every boundary

items.title: 014. The gate that refuses a change is defined once
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

The checks that gate a change are defined in exactly one runnable place, and the pipeline runs that same definition. What refuses a commit refuses a merge.
path: 014. The gate that refuses a change is defined once

items.title: Decision
items.text:
One definition, run at two moments. The gate — formatting, linting, typing, secret scanning, file well-formedness — exists once, as an artifact that can be run. The person committing runs it; the pipeline runs the same thing, not a second list written for it.

A rule cannot exist in one moment and not the other. Adding a rule is a single edit effective at both. Checks too expensive for the everyday moment (full suites, builds) run in the pipeline and are named as pipeline-only, not absent from the local gate with no mention of why.

This record settles where the gate is written and how often it runs; which findings it blocks is decided elsewhere (015).
path: 014. The gate that refuses a change is defined once

items.title: Context
items.text:
Every shipped change passes two moments of validation: the moment a person commits, the moment the pipeline reviews before merge. Both need the rules; the question is how many times the rules are written down.

Two written lists drift apart by their nature. A local script and a pipeline definition start identical and end apart, because whoever adds a rule usually thinks of one place. The drift costs in two ways:

  • The person whose change passes the first moment and fails the second pays a round trip through a pipeline run, and the lesson learned is that local passes mean nothing.

  • A gate discovered late trains people to treat the pipeline as the adversary rather than as evidence.

  • The team is small and multi-disciplinary: the people maintaining the rules are subject to them, so a rule kept in two places is maintained twice — which is how rules become inconsistent and then distrusted.

  • The repository spans several stacks: a gate defined per stack is several lists with several gaps, and the gap is where the next defect lands.
path: 014. The gate that refuses a change is defined once

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 One definition of the gate. The rule set exists once, as a runnable artifact — no second list kept in step by memory. R2 No rule discovered only in the pipeline. Passing locally means passing there, except checks explicitly named pipeline-only. R3 Cheap to keep true. A rule is one edit by the person who wants it, effective at both moments. R4 The gate is reviewable. The rule set is versioned, so a change to what is enforced is visible as a change. R5 Every stack is inside the gate. One definition covers every technology, so no stack is silently ungated.
path: 014. The gate that refuses a change is defined once

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails The pipeline as the only gate R1 and R4 pass, R2 fails by construction: every rule surfaces at its most expensive moment, after review time is spent, and the repair loop is a commit plus a run. It also lets bad form into history and complains afterwards. Two hand-maintained lists R1 outright, R3 with it: the lists are maintained by whoever remembers both, which over time is no one, and the drift is invisible until a change is caught in it. A gate per stack, wired per project R5: the gate becomes the union of what each stack adopted, and a new stack starts ungated. R3: a rule added "everywhere" is N edits. Do nothing (rules live in review comments) R1 by default: the rules exist in whoever reviews pull requests. R4: enforcement is a person's mood, and consistency scales with the reviewer's stamina.
path: 014. The gate that refuses a change is defined once

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 014. The gate that refuses a change is defined once

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• A person who can commit can merge — the pipeline adds no surprises of form (R2).
  • A rule is one edit that lands everywhere at once (R1, R3).
  • The rule set is a reviewed artifact: relaxing or tightening enforcement is visible history (R4).
  • Every stack enters the same gate (R5).
path: 014. The gate that refuses a change is defined once

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• The gate must run wherever people work, so its tooling must exist on every machine — a dependency on the versioned development environment (011), not on what a machine happens to have.
  • The gate must stay fast enough to run before every commit, or people start bypassing it. Gate runtime is a constraint to defend.
path: 014. The gate that refuses a change is defined once

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The pipeline-only checks are a standing exception that must stay named: a check that becomes cheap belongs local, a check that becomes slow belongs in the pipeline — each a reviewed edit to the definition.
  • The local gate runs against files a change touches; the pipeline runs it against the whole repository. A change to a shared rule (a lint config, a shared type) can pass locally and fail there: a second named exception to R2, not a hidden one. Whoever edits a shared rule file runs the gate across the repository before pushing.
Why not let the pipeline be the authority?

Because it makes the cheap lesson expensive. A rule that fires only in the pipeline costs a commit, a run, and a context switch — and teaches that local green means nothing. Moving discovery to commit time is the whole point of defining the gate once.
path: 014. The gate that refuses a change is defined once

items.title: 015. A change answers for what it caused
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

The checks that block a change are exactly the checks about the change itself. Findings about the state of the world are produced, recorded, and reviewed on a cadence — they do not block the change that surfaced them.
path: 015. A change answers for what it caused; the state of the world is reviewed on a cadence

items.title: Decision
items.text:
Blocking: the change's own findings. Form, lint, types, the tests and builds it can break, the absence of secrets it introduced. Advisory: the world's findings. Vulnerabilities in dependencies, code-quality measurements, coverage levels — produced on every change and on a schedule, recorded where they can be reviewed, not blocking the change that surfaced them.

The line is causation, not severity. A person is answerable at merge time for what their change did; the organisation is answerable on a cadence for the condition of everything it already ships. An advisory finding is not ignored — it is evidence for the review that consumes it — and a finding may be promoted to blocking when the organisation decides to hold changes to it.

This record settles which findings block a change; where the gate is defined is decided elsewhere (014).
path: 015. A change answers for what it caused; the state of the world is reviewed on a cadence

items.title: Context
items.text:
The organisation runs a growing set of checks — style, static analysis, types, tests, builds, secret scanning, vulnerability scanning, license review, quality analysis, coverage — and each produces findings. At merge time every finding raises the same question: does this stop this change?

Blocking on everything sounds safest and behaves worst. A vulnerability in a transitive dependency is not caused by the change under review and cannot be fixed by its author today; blocking on it punishes unrelated work, and the predictable response is to bypass the gate, re-run until green, or hold merges for someone to intervene. A gate trained to be bypassed stops enforcing the rules it was meant to keep. Coverage targets have their own failure: satisfied by uninformative tests, the number rises while the protection does not.

A gate trained to be bypassed

The decay this record is written against: block on everything and people route around the gate — re-run until green, bypass, hold merges — and the checks that catch real regressions lose their force. The blocking set stays small so that green is the normal outcome and a red gate means what it says.

Blocking on nothing is the opposite failure: findings accumulate because nothing forces anyone to look, and the organisation cannot say whether its shipments are getting safer or riskier. The team is small and multi-disciplinary — the same people write changes, see findings, and would absorb the triage — so the arrangement must work without a dedicated review function, and the blocking set must stay small enough to satisfy without ceremony.
path: 015. A change answers for what it caused; the state of the world is reviewed on a cadence

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 The blocking set is what the change caused. The author can satisfy every blocking check in their own change, without waiting for anyone's fix. R2 The everyday loop stays fast enough to keep. The blocking set runs on every change without dominating it. R3 Advisory findings are recorded, not discarded. Durable, attributable to the run, for whoever reviews system state. R4 The state of the world is examined on a schedule. Not only when a change touches the code that surfaces them. R5 Promotion is a decision. Advisory → blocking is deliberate and reviewable, so the blocking set stays small on purpose. R6 Cheap to keep true. A small team runs the whole arrangement with no dedicated triage role.
path: 015. A change answers for what it caused; the state of the world is reviewed on a cadence

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Block on everything R1: a finding about a dependency, a legacy file, or a coverage number is not the author's to fix, so merges stall on work someone else owes. R2 as the gate grows — and a gate that blocks the unfixable trains people to bypass it. Block on nothing R1's purpose: a change that introduces a secret or breaks a type reaches shared history. R3 in spirit: with no ceremony attached, the reports stop being read. Numeric thresholds as gates R1: the threshold measures the file, not the change — a legacy number blocks an unrelated fix. It buys the measured property, not the real one (a coverage floor is met by tests that assert nothing). R2: the cheapest response is lowering the threshold. Triage every finding before merge R3 passes, R6 fails: adjudication is standing work a small team cannot fund, and in practice it becomes a rubber stamp — the cost of triage with none of the attention. Do nothing (checks run, results unconsumed) R4 by default: scans tied to changes miss the world that changes nothing. R3: unclaimed reports decay into noise.
path: 015. A change answers for what it caused; the state of the world is reviewed on a cadence

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 015. A change answers for what it caused; the state of the world is reviewed on a cadence

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• Authors are stopped only by what they can fix, so the gate keeps its credibility and its speed (R1, R2).
  • The serious findings still arrive — per change and weekly — attached to the artifacts they describe, so the organisation can say what it knew and when (R3, R4).
  • The blocking set stays small because growing it is an explicit act (R5).
path: 015. A change answers for what it caused; the state of the world is reviewed on a cadence

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• Known vulnerabilities sit in shipped artifacts between finding and fix — risk carried deliberately, revisited on the cadence that produces the findings.
  • Nothing numeric forces quality upward: improvement depends on the review consuming the reports, not a gate enforcing it.
  • The promotion path is a decision the organisation keeps making, not a default it can rest on.
path: 015. A change answers for what it caused; the state of the world is reviewed on a cadence

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The cadence review is a standing obligation: the record's premise fails if the reviews stop happening — and naming the role that holds the review is the organisation's first act under this record. Until it is named, the review is unowned and the record is only half in force.
  • The weekly whole-system scan is the safety net for code that changes rarely.
  • Integrity checks that block (signed, attested releases) gate the release, not the change — left as they are.
  • A secret in history is unrecoverable, which is why secret scanning sits on the blocking side while vulnerability scanning does not.
Why not block on high-severity vulnerabilities?

Because severity doesn't fix them. The author can't patch a transitive dependency inside the change under review, so the block stalls the merge without closing the finding — and teaches everyone that the gate is an obstacle to route around. The finding belongs to the cadence review, which can schedule the fix.
path: 015. A change answers for what it caused; the state of the world is reviewed on a cadence

items.title: 016. The system observes itself; its operational data never leaves it
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Traces, metrics, and logs are produced and consumed inside the system, at one collection point the system runs itself. No operational data ships to a vendor: understanding the system requires nothing outside it.
path: 016. The system observes itself; its operational data never leaves it

items.title: Decision
items.text:
The running picture lives inside. Every part exports the same three signals — traces, metrics, logs — to one collection point that is part of the system, and the tools that read the picture run beside it. Nothing is shipped to a hosted service.

The rule follows the data to its source. A part running in a user's browser sends its signals to the collection point its deployment names, so a customer's deployment keeps the picture inside the same boundary. A part that emits nothing is a blind spot, treated as a defect, not a simplification.

The collection seam itself — one protocol, replaceable tools — is a separate decision (034); this record covers where the picture lives.
path: 016. The system observes itself; its operational data never leaves it

items.title: Context
items.text:
The behaviour of the business system lives in the conversations between its parts, so when something misbehaves, the evidence is spread across them: which request entered where, how long each hop took, what each part decided. The question is where the picture is assembled and who may hold its raw material.

The conventional answer moves the raw material outside. A hosted observability service is cheap to operate, and operational data is not neutral: traces carry request data, logs carry identifiers, and what they reveal about customers grows as the system grows. Once the data flows to a vendor, every environment needs an account, a network path, and a data-processing agreement — and an environment that cannot grant them (an offline machine, a restricted site, a demonstration) runs blind.

The system is meant to be legible wherever it runs: a person's machine, the pipeline, a customer's environment (006). And because the examples are how the organisation teaches (009), the debugging path is part of what is taught — if observing required an external account, the taught path would be one the learner cannot walk.
path: 016. The system observes itself; its operational data never leaves it

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 The picture is assembled inside. Signals from every part meet where the system runs; reading them needs nothing external. R2 The system runs where data may not leave. Running it can never depend on a third-party data agreement. R3 Observing needs no accounts or network. A person on their machine and an unattended run get the same picture. R4 The path is exercised where validation runs. The debugging path is live in local and pipeline runs, not discovered under pressure. R5 Cheap to keep true. Instrumenting a part, or adding the stack to an environment, is a local change.
path: 016. The system observes itself; its operational data never leaves it

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails A hosted observability service R2: the raw material leaves the boundary; R3: every environment needs an account and a network path, so an offline run loses the picture — contradicting 006. R4: the debugging path exists only where the vendor is reachable, so the taught path and the shipped path diverge. Self-hosted stack, outside the system R2 yes; R1 and R3 no: the picture is assembled where the system does not run, so every environment provisions the stack beside it — the account-and-network dependency with a different owner. R5: every new environment installs two things. The cloud platform's monitoring R2: the data leaves the boundary, to the platform's owner. R3 for every environment not on that platform. Logs only, no traces or metrics R2 and R3 pass, R1 fails: the picture of a request crossing several parts cannot be reassembled from uncorrelated text — precisely the failure mode the system's shape makes common. Each part exports to its own backend R1 in practice: a picture spread over unlinked backends is not one picture — and the seam those backends would sit behind is what 034 decides. Do nothing (prints and local reproduction) R1 by default: the evidence of an incident is whatever the logs happened to catch. R4: the debugging path is invented per incident, not exercised daily.
path: 016. The system observes itself; its operational data never leaves it

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 016. The system observes itself; its operational data never leaves it

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• The system is legible wherever it runs — offline, in a customer's environment — with no account to provision (R1, R3).
  • No operational data crosses the boundary, so running the system never requires a data-processing agreement (R2).
  • The debugging path is live in every validation run: trusted before it is needed (R4).
path: 016. The system observes itself; its operational data never leaves it

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• The organisation operates its own observation stack — availability, retention, dashboards are its problem; a hosted service's polish is paid for in upkeep.
  • The picture is bounded by what a self-hosted stack at the scale of the run can hold: long retention and fleet-wide aggregation are not on offer.
  • Every part that ships uninstrumented is a blind spot its owner must close — the picture is only as complete as its least-instrumented part.
path: 016. The system observes itself; its operational data never leaves it

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• Parts that currently emit nothing are deviations this record names rather than tolerates: each needs instrumentation or a stated reason not to have it. A part emitting only some of the three signals is a partial blind spot, treated the same way.
  • The collection point speaks a standard protocol (034) so a future production arrangement may export elsewhere — no export may begin without a new record superseding this one.
  • Sampling rates are a tuning decision per part; how long signals are kept is a lifetime question owned by 025.
Why not a hosted service for production only?

Because the rule is about the system, not the environment. A production export splits the debugging path in two — the legible arrangement taught locally, an opaque one where it matters most — and the split is exactly what 006 removes elsewhere. Export requires superseding this record first.
path: 016. The system observes itself; its operational data never leaves it

items.title: 017. Shared concepts change only in ways that keep readers working
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

A change to a shared concept must leave every existing reader working without being changed first. Additive change is the default; a breaking change is a new version carried beside the old one, never an edit to what readers consume.
path: 017. Shared concepts change only in ways that keep readers working

items.title: Decision
items.text:
The compatibility rule sets the direction. A concept change is permitted only where it leaves every existing reader of the concept working unmodified. Additive change — a new optional element — is the default direction; a change that would break a reader is a new version, carried alongside the old one for a stated period, never an edit to what readers already consume.

The rule is checked where it can be checked — a violating change is refused, not warned about — and where it cannot yet be checked, the change carries the same obligation by review.

This record settles the direction concepts may move in; where the canonical definition lives and how copies are kept honest is decided elsewhere (004).
path: 017. Shared concepts change only in ways that keep readers working

items.title: Context
items.text:
Business concepts are consumed the moment they are defined: records carrying them sit in streams waiting to be read, rows persist for years, and receivers outside the organisation parse them on their own schedule. A concept has consumers the organisation does not control and cannot pause — data in motion, data stored, partners integrated.

That is what separates concept change from code change. Code and its callers are updated together in one change; a concept's older readers cannot be updated before the change lands, because they run elsewhere or the data they read was written earlier. A concept edited in a breaking direction does not fail at the edit — it fails later, at whichever reader cannot parse what arrived, far from the change that caused it.

One canonical definition per concept (004) made every consumer depend on one statement — that is the point — which means the statement now needs a rule for how it may change: a single definition edited freely concentrates exactly the breakage it was meant to prevent. The guidance so far recommends a compatibility strategy without naming who enforces it or what a genuine break becomes, so the rule lives nowhere and every concept change re-decides it.

Why the rule is about concepts, not code

A code change and its callers ship together, so a break fails the build. A concept — a type's meaning, an enum's set, a field's shape — is read by data written yesterday and by processes the release does not reach. The edit passes every check; the failure happens later, at a reader far from the change. That lag is why compatibility needs its own rule, and why the single canonical definition (004) concentrates the breakage it needs to prevent.
path: 017. Shared concepts change only in ways that keep readers working

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 Existing readers keep working. Every reader built against the earlier version still reads what arrives, unmodified. R2 Old data stays readable. Records written before the change remain parseable afterwards, as long as they exist. R3 Breakage is a new version, not an edit. The old version keeps being served while the new is adopted, with a stated path and period. R4 The rule is enforced, not advised. A violating change is stopped by a check, not left to whoever remembers. R5 The rule is stated where consumers can read it. What may change and what is stable, without asking anyone. R6 Cheap to keep true. Honouring the rule costs a small routine step, not a ceremony.
path: 017. Shared concepts change only in ways that keep readers working

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Free change: edit whenever needed R1 and R2 by construction: readers built against the old shape meet data they cannot parse, stored records become unreadable — the failure lands at the worst time, far from its cause. R5: nothing tells a consumer when the ground moved. Freeze: no breaking changes ever R3's purpose: businesses do need changes readers cannot absorb — a removed field, a retyped identifier — and a rule with no exit is quietly abandoned the first time one is needed, taking the rest of the rule with it. Warn but don't stop R4: a warning that merges anyway is the same arrangement as no rule, differing only in logs. R5: "ask the elders" is not a stated rule. Version everything up front R1 and R2 pass, R6 fails: the routine majority (additive changes) would each spawn a parallel version to maintain. R5 degrades: consumers face a version matrix where one evolving concept would serve. Do nothing (keep recommending a strategy) Where the repository stands, so it costs nothing. R4 by default: the recommendation has no enforcement point. R3: no stated path for the breaking change guidance cannot prevent.
path: 017. Shared concepts change only in ways that keep readers working

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 017. Shared concepts change only in ways that keep readers working

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• Concept changes stop being an incident risk: readers built earlier keep working, so streams and stored data survive the change (R1, R2).
  • The rare breaking need has a named route instead of an exception made under pressure (R3).
  • Consumers integrate against a stated contract, not an observed habit (R5).
path: 017. Shared concepts change only in ways that keep readers working

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• The everyday direction of change is widened rather than deepened: reshaping a concept is a versioned migration — slower than an edit, and honestly sometimes felt as bureaucracy.
  • Running two versions side by side is real cost that must end on a stated date or become permanent.
  • Enforcement needs a checking mechanism the organisation does not fully have yet; until it exists the rule leans on review — a gap to close, not a tolerated state.
path: 017. Shared concepts change only in ways that keep readers working

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The compatibility level at which the registry refuses changes is this rule's enforcement point and must be set deliberately, not inherited from a default — until set, R4 is aspirational at that boundary.
  • Hand-kept representations of a concept are checked against this rule by review until a check exists — the obligation 004 already carries. Storage sinks configured not to follow concept changes are deliberate; keeping table and concept in step is then a named migration task.
  • The period an old version runs alongside a new one is named by the concept's owner at the time of the break, not later.
  • Dependent set — records that lean on this rule without restating it: 027 (how a stream behaves), 030 (interfaces verified against this rule), 032 (the name a breaking change travels under). If this record is superseded, those three are the set to re-check.
Why carry two versions instead of a migration window?

Because the readers are outside. A migration window works when you control both ends and can schedule the cutover; here the data is in streams, stored rows, and partner systems that parse on their own schedule. The old version keeps answering them while the new one is adopted on their clock, not the editor's.
path: 017. Shared concepts change only in ways that keep readers working

items.title: 018. Settings arrive at startup through one channel and fail loudly
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

Every setting a part needs arrives through the environment it starts in and is validated once, at startup. A missing setting stops the start; nothing environment-specific is compiled into a part.
path: 018. Settings arrive at startup through one channel and fail loudly

items.title: Decision
items.text:
One channel: the start-up environment. Addresses, ports, feature switches, credentials a part reads rather than owns — all arrive through the environment the part starts in, read and validated once, at startup. A part that has started has been told everything it needs and found it usable; a missing or malformed setting stops the start rather than surfacing at first use.

Nothing environment-specific is compiled in. The validated unit is reconfigured per environment by changing what it is told, never by rebuilding — which is what makes 010 possible at all.

The channel is defined by who supplies the settings — the deployment — not by the delivery mechanism: a part rendered in a browser cannot read a server's environment, so its deployment places the settings beside it for pickup at run start, the same channel one step removed. Where a setting is a secret, this record governs how it arrives, not where it rests (008).
path: 018. Settings arrive at startup through one channel and fail loudly

items.title: Context
items.text:
Parts are configured by different forces: an engineer changes a port to avoid a collision, the pipeline points a part at a throwaway service, a deployment points it at the real one. The settings belong to the part; the values belong to the environment. Every stack in the repository has its own historical habit for how a value reaches code — a compiled-in file per environment, a settings document, a value read deep in a request path — and each habit carries the same two costs.

  • The rebuild trap. A setting fixed at build time makes a new environment a new build, quietly breaking the rule that the validated unit is the deployed unit: the deployment then carries a build no validation ever saw.
  • Late failure. A setting read when first used fails at an ordinary-looking moment, far from the start that omitted it. A part that starts broken and fails at first use is worse to operate than one that refuses to start: the second is obvious, the first is a support ticket.

The team is small, multi-disciplinary, and moves between stacks — a different configuration habit per stack is a different habit to remember per stack, and the person debugging a misconfigured part at two in the afternoon does not care which ecosystem the part was written in.
path: 018. Settings arrive at startup through one channel and fail loudly

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Any acceptable arrangement must deliver:

Requirement R1 One channel for every stack. A setting reaches a part the same way in every technology — one mental model. R2 Reconfiguring never rebuilds. A new environment changes only what the part is told; the validated unit is untouched. R3 Bad settings fail at startup. A missing or malformed setting stops the start, naming the setting. R4 The running configuration is knowable. What a part was told can be enumerated from outside — a fact, not a hypothesis. R5 Configuration and secrets stay distinct. Ordinary settings may be committed dev defaults; secrets follow 008. R6 Cheap to keep true. Adding a setting is a local edit to the part and its environment description.
path: 018. Settings arrive at startup through one channel and fail loudly

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Alternative Why it fails Compile settings in per environment R2 outright: every environment becomes its own build, taking the confidence transfer 010 with it. R1 in spirit: the environment's values live in the build system, not with the environment. A central configuration service R1 and R4 elegantly; the arrangement the system runs under, no: every start waits on a service and a network (006), so offline and unattended runs need a fallback — a local file — and the organisation now has two channels and has decided nothing. Settings files beside the code, read at will R2: the file travels inside the unit, so environment values ship inside the artifact. R3: a value read at first use fails at first use. R1: the mechanism is whatever each stack's library offers. Framework defaults with silent fallbacks R3 by design: a missing setting is indistinguishable from an intentional default, so a part pointed at the wrong place by omission looks healthy until it writes somewhere wrong. Do nothing (each stack keeps its habit) The current state, costs nothing. R1 by default: every stack answers the same question differently. R3 unevenly — some habits fail loudly and some don't, which is worse than all failing loudly.
path: 018. Settings arrive at startup through one channel and fail loudly

items.title: Tradeoffs
path: 018. Settings arrive at startup through one channel and fail loudly

items.title: What it buys
items.text:
• One question — "what was this part told at startup?" — answers configuration for every stack (R1, R4).
  • Environments differ by values, never by builds, so the deployment rule holds (R2).
  • A misconfigured part is loud at start instead of quiet at first use (R3); adding a setting is local work (R6).
path: 018. Settings arrive at startup through one channel and fail loudly

items.title: What it costs
items.text:
• The environment description joins every run path, so a typo in an environment file becomes the commonest incident — the correct trade, but the incidents are real.
  • Startup validation must be written deliberately for each part: a part that merely reads strings discovers its problems late.
path: 018. Settings arrive at startup through one channel and fail loudly

items.title: Watch
items.text:
• The browser-rendered part fetches its settings at run start, which is the same channel one step removed — it needs the same startup-validation habit to be worth anything. The example now validates the fetched document at bootstrap and fails loudly (apps/aurelius-atlas-frontend-example/src/app/config.ts) — the deviation this record named is closed.
  • The Node-RED example that baked its production settings into its unit left with its slice (050).
  • The setting/secret line is enforced by the check 008 already owes. The startup message's quality is a standing obligation: the enumerated startup configuration is where an operational review looks first.
Why not a configuration service — live settings, one source?

Because every start would then wait on it. The offline laptop and the unattended pipeline run need the part to start with what it was given (006), so the service would need a local fallback — and a fallback file plus a service is two channels, which is the state this record exists to end.
path: 018. Settings arrive at startup through one channel and fail loudly

items.title: 019. The system releases as one versioned whole
items.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-07
  • Deciders: Aurelius Enterprise

One version number, one changelog, one release event that publishes every deployable part. A released version is a complete, mutually consistent snapshot; parts are not independently versioned or released.
path: 019. The system releases as one versioned whole

items.title: Decision
items.text:
The system is the unit of release. One version number, one changelog, one release event publishing every deployable part together. A released version is a complete, mutually consistent snapshot — every part in it was built and validated against the same everything.

Parts move with the system, not beside it. When a part changes, the system's version moves; the changelog records which parts moved and how.

This is the delivery face of two older decisions: the single repository makes one version meaningful (001), and the unit that ships is the unit that was validated (010) — lockstep release keeps those true at the moment of delivery, not only at the moment of commit.
path: 019. The system releases as one versioned whole

items.title: Context
items.text:
The repository holds many deployable things — services, frontends, functions, connectors — useful only in combination: a frontend that speaks to a service that reads what a producer writes. The question is what gets a version number and a release: each part separately, or the system as a whole.

Independent per-part versioning is what per-part packaging encourages, and it is paid for in compatibility knowledge.
